World.title: I ignored warnings before backing Gbenga Daniel for Senate in 2023 – Abiodun
World.content:
Gov. Abiodun

Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun has disclosed that he was advised not to support former governor and current senator representing Ogun East, Gbenga Daniel, for the Senate during the 2023 general election because of fears that the former governor might later oppose him politically.

The governor made the revelation while receiving members of Daniel’s political family and loyalists of the late Senator Buruji Kashamu into the mainstream of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Abeokuta.

In a statement issued on Thursday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Kayode Akinmade, Abiodun described the return of the political groups as an important development that would strengthen the APC ahead of the 2027 elections.

Reflecting on the political events of 2023, the governor said he was cautioned against supporting Daniel’s emergence as the APC senatorial candidate because of concerns that the former governor could eventually turn against him.

“Despite the warnings, I supported Daniel because of my respect for him as a former governor and my belief that political disagreements should not diminish the respect accorded former occupants of the office.

“I just decided that we should honour him because one day, I will also become a former governor.”

Abiodun also recalled a political meeting during which, according to him, Daniel expressed uncertainty over who would become the next governor of Ogun State, despite one of the contenders belonging to his political party.

“Now the gloves are off. He is the same person that we heard in an audio saying he had taken someone to court,” Abiodun added.

The governor further expressed concern over what he described as the recent relaunch of Daniel’s foundation, where the Peoples Democratic Party governorship candidate, Hon. Ladi Adebutu, was reportedly a special guest of honour.

According to Abiodun, the development appeared to indicate that Daniel had chosen to operate outside the mainstream of the APC, despite remaining a respected political figure in Ogun State.

He said his relationship with the former governor had always been guided by respect for the office of governor and the status of former office holders.

“You know OGD is my leader because he was governor before me. I joined Ogun State politics way before him. Without a doubt, I was a senator-elect in the state in 1996/1997,” Abiodun said.

The governor also reflected on his political journey and cautioned against the misuse of political power.

“You don’t begin to act as if you are God. You don’t begin to play as if you are an emperor. God gives us power and looks at how we use it. If you utilise it very well, God will leave it with you for a long time to continue to wield it. If you abuse it, God will take it away from you and give it to somebody else,” he said.

At the meeting held at the Presidential Lodge in Abeokuta, Abiodun commended the defectors for aligning with the APC and urged politicians with shared interests to speak with one voice rather than work for different political parties.

In response, Daniel’s media aide, Steve Oliyide, denied that the former governor had relaunched any foundation, insisting that the gathering was merely a reunion of old and new members of the Gateway Front Foundation ahead of its 25th anniversary.

“There was no ‘relaunch’of the Foundation yet, but a reunion of old and new members of the Gateway Front Foundation to plan for its 25th Anniversary. I am not sure if there was ever any need for a Special Guest of Honour at such an event.

“Hon. Ladi Adebutu is also an old member of the Foundation, except the writer is asking that an old member of over 20 years should be excused from an event in which he played a significant role simply because of his political ambition to please some other people.”

Daniel’s media office had earlier distanced the senator from a circulating audio recording, describing it as manipulated and fabricated.

“The OGD Media Office has been inundated with enquiries regarding a purportedly leaked private conversation allegedly involving His Excellency, Otunba Gbenga Daniel, and a respected elder statesman.

“For the records, this Office became aware of the existence of the audio over six weeks ago, following attempts by its purveyors to deploy the maliciously doctored recording as an instrument of political blackmail, coercion, intimidation, and other criminal ends.

“The audio in circulation is a manipulated and deliberately doctored material, calculated to mislead the public, malign the reputation of His Excellency, and advance a premeditated political agenda.

“Accordingly, the appropriate law enforcement agencies have been formally invited to investigate the source of the recording, those responsible for its manipulation and dissemination, and the criminal motives behind its circulation.

“In addition, our legal team has been instructed to pursue all available civil and criminal remedies against every individual or group connected with this orchestrated campaign of calumny, defamation, malicious falsehood, and cybercrime.This shenanigans must stop in our body politics.”

The exchange comes amid growing political tension between Abiodun and Daniel over the 2027 Ogun East senatorial ticket. Daniel is reportedly seeking another term in the Senate, while Abiodun, who will complete his second term as governor next year, is also believed to be interested in the seat.

The APC has since adopted Abiodun as its consensus candidate for the 2027 Ogun East Senate race, and he was subsequently declared winner of the party’s primary election.

World.title: 2 African countries qualify for 2027 Women World Cup playoffs
World.content:
Ghana and South Africa have secured Africa’s two places in the inter-confederation play-offs for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup after both countries recorded crucial victories in Casablanca on Thursday.

The Black Queens booked their place first after coming from behind to defeat Côte d’Ivoire 2-1.

Inès Konan put the Elephants ahead from the penalty spot in the fourth minute, giving Côte d’Ivoire an early advantage.

Ghana responded strongly after the break, with Princess Marfo restoring parity before Josephine Bonsu completed the comeback with 18 minutes remaining.

The victory sent the Black Queens through to the 10-team inter-confederation play-offs, where they will battle for one of the three remaining World Cup places.

South Africa then joined Ghana after defeating Nigeria 2-1 in the later fixture.

The Super Falcons had been hoping to keep their World Cup qualification record intact, but Banyana Banyana secured the crucial victory to end Nigeria’s hopes of reaching the tournament for the first time in their history.

South Africa’s victory means the two-time WAFCON champions will represent Africa alongside Ghana in the inter-confederation play-offs.

The play-offs will be held across two international windows between November 2026 and February 2027, with the 10 participating teams divided into three mini-tournaments.

The winners of the three mini-tournaments will secure the final three places at next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Ghana and South Africa will therefore have another opportunity to secure their places at the global tournament after missing out on direct qualification through the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations route.

Vanguard News

World.title: Police mopped up 34 illegal weapons in Osun ahead poll – Force PRO
World.content:
File image.

By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

The Nigeria Police Force has disclosed that it has mopped up 34 illegal firearms ahead of the governorship election in Osun State.

This was disclosed by the Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Aniete Iniedu, while fielding questions from stakeholders at the town hall meeting held at the Osun State police command headquarters in Osogbo on Thursday.

He said investigation is ongoing into the sources of the weapons after which the illegal owners will be prosecuted in line with the directives of the Inspector General of Police.

“With regards to illicit weapons, about 34 recovered arms in Osun State ahead of the election. Investigation is ongoing about it, after which there will be prosecution”, he said.

CSP Iniedu further disclosed that illicit weapons were not allowed at the polling units.

“Even the four policemen that were deployed to each unit will not carry weapons. All kind of firearms or any weapon is prohibited at the polling units in line with the Electoral Acts.

“What we will do is that apart from the uniformed officers deployed at the unit, secret police officers and other security agents will be at the polling units to profile voters and the people present at polling units,” he said.

The Force PRO had earlier disclosed that apart from the 15,000 policemen deployed to the state, police helicopter and drone units have also arrived the state to conduct aerial surveillance before, during and immediately after the election.

World.title: South Africa beat Nigeria 2-1 to end Super Falcons’ World Cup hopes
World.content:
Super Falcons

South Africa defeated Nigeria 2-1 in Casablanca on Thursday to secure a place in the Inter-Confederation Playoff preliminary round for next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

The defeat ended the Super Falcons’ hopes of qualifying for the tournament for the first time in their history.

Nigeria entered the decisive encounter after suffering a 1-0 defeat to Cameroon in the quarter-finals of the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations, while South Africa were beaten 2-1 by hosts Morocco at the same stage.

With both teams needing victory to keep their World Cup hopes alive, South Africa took the lead through Thembi Kgatlana before captain Refiloe Jane doubled Banyana Banyana’s advantage in the second half.

Nigeria struggled to find a way through South Africa’s defence despite creating several opportunities, with goalkeeper Kaylin Swart making crucial saves to keep her side ahead.

The Super Falcons were handed a lifeline late in the game when Jane was sent off after a handball resulted in a penalty for Nigeria.

Christy Ucheibe converted the spot-kick to reduce the deficit to 2-1 and give Nigeria hope of completing a comeback.

However, South Africa held on during six minutes of stoppage time to secure a crucial victory.

The result means Banyana Banyana advance to the six-team Inter-Confederation Playoff preliminary round, where they will compete for one of three available places at the 2027 Women’s World Cup.

The top two teams from the preliminary round will advance alongside four teams that have received byes. The winners of the three final-round ties will then qualify for the World Cup in Brazil.

For Nigeria, however, the defeat brings an end to their hopes of appearing at the tournament and marks the first time the Super Falcons have failed to qualify for the FIFA Women’s World Cup.

South Africa’s victory follows Ghana’s 2-1 win over Côte d’Ivoire earlier on Thursday, which also secured the Black Queens a place in the Inter-Confederation Playoff preliminary round.

Vanguard News

World.title: 2027: Makinde names ex-SSS DG Lawal Daura as running mate
World.content:
Presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Seyi Makinde, has selected former Director-General of the State Security Service (SSS), Lawal Daura, as his running mate for the 2027 presidential election.

Daura, who led the SSS from 2015 to 2018, was unveiled as Makinde’s vice-presidential candidate during the party’s national convention held at Rilwan Adamu Square in Bauchi on Thursday.

The announcement was contained in a statement issued by the Oyo State Commissioner for Information, Prince Dotun Oyelade, who said Makinde intentionally chose the former intelligence chief because of the country’s growing security concerns.

“His Presidential running mate is Alh. Lawal Musa Daura, the former Director-General of the State Security Service (SSS) between 2015 and 2018, whom he said was deliberately chosen to solve the security situation of the country,” the statement read.

Daura served as SSS director-general under former President Muhammadu Buhari before he was removed from office in 2018.

Makinde was formally elected as the APM presidential candidate at the convention and used the occasion to promise collaboration with politicians who share his vision for national development.

“The APM Presidential candidate said that he will work actively with like-minded politicians to ensure a better Nigeria come 2027,” the statement added.

The Oyo State governor also said he was ready to tackle poverty and improve the living conditions of millions of Nigerians, arguing that recent economic difficulties had been worsened by ineffective policies.

“Gov. Makinde said he’s well prepared to lift the millions of Nigerians out of the poverty level, which has ravaged the land even more in the past three years as a result of poorly implemented policies,” Oyelade stated.

Makinde further explained that Bauchi was chosen for the convention because of its historical importance as the home state of Nigeria’s first Prime Minister, Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.

World.title: Just in: Trump announces tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones
World.content:
File image

President Donald Trump announced on Thursday tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports of unmanned drones and their components to reduce US reliance on imports in an industry dominated by China.

The US president justified the decision on national security grounds, according to a White House statement, detailing a 100 percent duty rate on the import of certain unmanned aircraft systems, including those with a take-off weight of more than 25 kilograms and with national security capabilities such as thermal imagers and docking stations.

Smaller drones face a 25 percent tariff.

The statement said the tariffs will “encourage increased domestic production” of drones and their components and reduce reliance on foreign supply chains.

The Chinese company DJI, founded in 2006, has captured more than two-thirds of the global drone market in recent years, according to several studies.

Most of the new tariffs duties are take effect September 3.

Last week, China announced restrictions on drone exports to the United States and blacklisted six companies in response to trade sanctions imposed by Washington over forced labor and national security concerns.

That move came days after the US imposed fresh tariffs on China and 59 countries.

AFP

World.title: Nigeria, US reinforce strategic defence, security partnership at Washington talks
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa (Rtd), has concluded high-level bilateral engagements with United States authorities in Washington DC, aimed at deepening military-to-military relations and fortifying counter-terrorism cooperation between both nations.

A statement by Leah Katung Babatunde, SA Media to the Minister said, “During a strategic meeting at the Pentagon, the Defence Minister was joined by a high-powered Nigerian delegation that included Mr. Taiwo Oyedele the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, General Olufemi Oluyede the Chief of Defence Staff, Lt. General Parker Udiandeye the Chief of Defence Intelligence and other Senior Officers from the Armed Forces of Nigeria.

“The Nigerian delegation held robust discussions with senior cabinet officials of the U.S. Department of War led by Julia Sokol, Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for International Security Affairs.

“The engagement served as a direct continuation of the United States–Nigeria Joint Working Group Defence Bilateral Talks, focusing on shared security architecture, intelligence collaboration, and operational synergies.

“The diplomatic mission, led by the National Security Adviser (NSA), Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, is made of senior government officials, who are in the United States of America for the second meeting of the US–Nigeria Joint Working Group, held from August 12 to 13, 2026.

“Co-chaired by Mallam Nuhu Ribadu and Allison Hooker, the U.S. Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, the meeting reviewed actionable progress and strategic frameworks following Nigeria’s designation as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC). Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to sustained dialogue, mutual respect, and strategic alliance in combating global and regional threats.”

World.title: UAE condemns Iranian attack on two vessels in Hormuz strait
World.content:
The United Arab Emirates on Friday condemned an Iranian attack it said targeted two vessels linked to state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) as they passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, which the US fiercely opposes. Iran is in talks with Oman over arrangements for the strait’s future management.

The UAE foreign ministry in a statement denounced what it called “the hostile Iranian attack that targeted two vessels affiliated with ADNOC as they transited the Strait of Hormuz, with no injuries reported”.

ADNOC confirmed “two of its vessels were attacked while transiting” the waterway on Thursday evening, adding the situation was “brought under control”, the official WAM news agency reported.

AFP

World.title: Osun Election: Over 1.9m Voters to Decide Adeleke, Oyebamiji, Salaam, Other’s Fate Saturday
World.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

Ahead of the Osun State governorship election scheduled for Saturday, a total of 1,906,390 voters will decide the fate of the 15 governorship candidates in the election.

Recall that the leading candidates including the incumbent Governor and the candidate of Accord Senator Ademola Adeleke, Bola Oyebamiji of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and Dr. Najeem Salaam of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) on Tuesday at the Arise News town hall offered their visions for the state.

While Adeleke defended his three-and-a-half-year record, Oyebamiji presented himself as an investment and public finance expert capable of turning around the state’s economy, whereas Salaam promised to revive social programmes associated with earlier administrations and create 20,000 jobs within his first 100 days in office.

However, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) Thursday announced the final figures of the Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) collected by registered voters across the State.

INEC National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Haruna in a statement issued revealed that out of the total of 2,339,233 registered voters in the State, 1,906,390 PVCs, representing 81.50 per cent, have been collected.

He added that the remaining 426,842 PVCs, representing 18.50 per cent, have been safely deposited with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), in line with the Commission’s established practice.

Haruna noted: “Similarly, it should be noted that some persons with damaged, defaced, or lost PVCs applied for replacement of their cards.

“A total of 6,101 among those who applied printed downloadable copies of their PVCs. A table of the PVCs collected, Polling Unit by Polling Unit (PU), has been published on the Commission’s website.”

The Commission reassured political parties, civil society organisations, media, and the good people of Osun State of its total readiness to conduct a free, fair, credible, transparent, and inclusive election.

World.title: Tinubu: Fuel Subsidy Removal Benefitting Ordinary Nigerians
World.content:
.Promises to publish how subsidy savings are utilised

.Optimistic nation’s four moribund refineries will be back on stream and make profit

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu on Thursday disclosed that the fuel subsidy removal, which he announced upon his inauguration as President on May 29, 2023, actually benefitted ordinary Nigerians. Speaking while receiving in audience the newly elected leadership of Nigeria Union of Petroleum and Natural Gas Workers (NUPENG) at the State House, Abuja, Tinubu explained that the fuel subsidy removal is actually benefitting ordinary Nigerians.



He gave an assurance that his government will soon publish details of how the savings from the fuel subsidy withdrawal are being utilised and cited regular salary payments and funding for major road projects as some benefits of the policy.

Tinubu said: “Fuel subsidy is gone for the benefit of our great country. I will soon publish the utilization of what it is. I listen to people, they say common man and all of that. Who are the people receiving the salaries in the local government administration? Are they not common men and women receiving salary regularly at the state level, are they not common men and women? The ordinary people receiving salary at the federal government regularly, and it affects all the market women around us, including your wives.



“But I’m glad you have seen the effect of being able to find funding for long-term projects; Lagos-Ibadan Road, Abuja-Kaduna highway, Abuja-Kano, and Sokoto-Badagry highways and many other road network, it’s all for the good of us and the good of our economy and the safety of our people.”

The President also expressed optimism that the nation’s four moribund refineries will be back to operation, stressing, however, that it must be commercially viable.

According to Tinubu: “The refineries that you mentioned is going to come back to work. We’re just building a very firm reset and structural reworking of the economic of it. Ordinary flame and smoke of refinery doesn’t mean that it’s working until it’s profitable and yield the value for which it is built.



“I’ve accepted the asset and liability of my predecessors, no matter what has happened in the years past, it’s my responsibility now as the president to fix it, make it work for the largest common value of our population. I take responsibility for that, and I’m going to do it.”

The President also told NUPENG leadership to impress it upon their members to pass benefits from CNG on to commuters so that it can go round the citizenry.



His words: “Equally, the introduction of compressed natural gas. Well, I will appeal to you, we will do more. We will encourage you, but ask your drivers to let it trickle to the commuters too, because whatever benefit that is coming from CNG is going to the pocket of truck owners. It’s not spreading as fast as I would like it, but it should spread.”

Earlier, NUPENG President, Comrade Akanni Oladiti, appealed to President Tinubu to check casualisation of workers in the oil industry in the country.



Oladiti, who described the trend as unwholesome, expressed concern that efforts to make the oil companies involved, particularly in the upstream oil and gas sector to shelve the practice have been constantly rebuffed.

His words:”Your Excellency, our relationship with the International Oil Companies and the indigenous players in the upstream sector has been very cordial. However, we want to seize this opportunity to bring to your attention an unhealthy trend we have been trying to correct with little to no success. It is the casualisation of workers, particularly in the upstream sector.

“For a sector that is strategic and taken as the economic jugular of the nation, NUPENG and its counterpart, the PENGASSAN have been tolerating these unwholesome practices, knowing full well the enormous disruption that any industrial actions could cause to the economy.



“We also do not want to be seen to be hostile to the Minister of Labour, Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi, who has been very supportive and operates an open-door policy in his relationship with our Union.

“We have engaged the management of some of the affected companies without results. Mr. President, we urge you to use your good offices to stop casualisation of workers in our sector.”

While commending the federal government for its rehabilitation and dualisation of highways to ease movement of petroleum trucks, Oladiti also appealed to the President to see to rescucitate the Nigerian Pipelines and Storage Company (NPSC) depots nationwide as well as the four refineries in the country.



According to him, injecting life into the depots would complement the ongoing positive step to revive the ailing refineries.

Said he:” We’ve seen real progress in the rehabilitation of federal highways, making

journeys safer for our tanker drivers.

“Mr. President, your administration has turned federal highways into massive construction sites. We must not fail to mention the ongoing, unprecedented projects, 750- kilometer, six lane Lagos – Coastal Highway and the 1,068- kilometer Sokoto- Badagry Superhighway that will traverse seven states in the

country.



“For our members, a good road is the difference between arriving home safely and never arriving at all. Every stretch of highway rehabilitated or constructed, means fewer accidents, fewer spillages,

fewer lives lost, and lesser stress for the men behind the wheel. Mr. President, that is a reform our members feel in their bones, and for it we say thank you.



“We also want to commend your administration’s move to revive the Warri and Port Harcourt refineries through partnership with Chinese firms.

Your Excellency, we want to humbly request that the same energy and drive to inject life back to the refineries be extended to the decaying Nigerian Pipelines and Storage Company (NPSC) depots of

country.



“We strongly recommend they can be handed over to private investors to manage under an equity arrangement.”

The NUPENG boss also urged President Tinubu to promote grassroots development by ensuring that state governors comply with the Supreme Court judgment on financial autonomy for the local governments

World.title: We Must Remain Resilient, Drug War is a Generational Task, Marwa Charges NDLEA Officers
World.content:
Honours 274 personnel, 18 Commands, 19 NGOs, media platforms at 12th awards ceremony in Abuja

The Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA), Brig. Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa (Rtd.) has charged officers, men and women of the anti-narcotics institution to remain resilient in view of the persistent nature of the drug challenge, which he described as a generational responsibility.

He gave the charge on Thursday 13th August 2026 during the 12th Chairman/Chief Executive Officer’s Commendations and Awards ceremony at the Agency’s national headquarters in Abuja where he honoured 274 personnel for outstanding performance in the discharge of their duties, and 18 best-performing commands as well as 19 NGOs and media organisations for their commitment to the war against drug abuse (WADA) advocacy in Nigeria.

According to him, “the war against illicit drugs is not a campaign with an end date. It is a generational responsibility. For every cartel we dismantle, intelligence tells us another will attempt to rise. For every corridor we shut down, traffickers will search for another route.”

He explained that the fight against drug trafficking could never be won by enforcement alone, noting that NGOs work quietly within communities to walk young people back from the edge of addiction, while journalists have told difficult stories on trafficking routes, rehabilitation, and family recovery that are not always easy to tell.

He acknowledged that many more deserving organisations and media platforms across the country exist beyond the honourees, describing the gesture as “the beginning of a tradition, not a closed chapter,” and assuring that subsequent editions of the ceremony will continue to identify and honour more individuals and organisations doing similar work.

“The fight against drug trafficking and substance abuse was never going to be won by enforcement alone. It is won in the communities where NGOs quietly walk young people back from the edge of addiction. It is won in the newsrooms where journalists chose to tell the difficult stories, the stories of trafficking routes, of rehabilitation, of families rebuilding, even when those stories were not the easiest to tell. Our partners in civil society and the media have been the multiplier effect on everything this Agency does. You have taken our message into homes, schools, and communities that our uniforms alone could never reach.”

Marwa highlighted some recent major operations that he said captured the character of the Agency: the dismantling of the Amadi Simon drug cartel; the takedown of two Nigerian-Mexican methamphetamine cartels operating within forests in Ogun and Oyo States; and the disruption of a tramadol cartel exploiting the Togo–Benin Republic–Nigeria corridor, which he described as a route that had for years fed a crisis of opioid abuse among Nigerian youth.

“These were not simple raids. They were the product of patient intelligence-gathering, cross-border cooperation, and officers willing to go where the criminals believed no one would follow”, he noted.

The NDLEA boss charged officers of the Agency to see the honourees as a standard to reach for rather than a ceiling to stop at, and urged partners in civil society and the media to view the recognition as an invitation to do more, not a reward to rest on.

He congratulated all recipients of awards and commendations, and thanked their families as well as Nigerians who continue to place their trust in the Agency.

World.title: OSUN: LET THE ELECTION BE PEACEFUL
World.content:
The Osun State election scheduled for Saturday, 15th August 2026, is an important moment in the political history of our dear state. It is therefore my sincere appeal that the election must be peaceful, free, fair, credible and transparent. Politics must never become a reason for brothers and sisters to fight, communities to be divided, lives to be lost or properties to be destroyed. Recent reports have raised concerns about election-related violence ahead of the poll and this makes the responsibility of every stakeholder even more required. Since the people of Osun State have the constitutional right to choose their governor, I appeal to all registered voters to go out and vote peacefully, vote for the candidate whose vision, character, competence and programme you believe can best serve Osun State.

The Independent National Electoral Commission must remain neutral, transparent, professional. The counting, collation and transmission of results must be handled transparently and where there are challenges, INEC must communicate clearly with the public. In the same vein, The Nigeria Police Force, Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps, military personnel and other security agencies deployed for the election have a critical responsibility. They must be reminded that their duty is to protect the people and the electoral process—not to serve the interests of any political party. Therefore, Security must be provided for all citizens, irrespective of political affiliation since the essence of democracy is that the people should be allowed to choose their leaders freely.

I also appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to allow INEC to carry out its constitutional responsibilities independently without interference. The actions, statements and body language of Mr. President matter greatly in building public confidence in the electoral process and the conduct and outcome of Osun state election will also be a template for general election next year.

John Tosin Ajiboye, Osogbo, Osun State

Letter2

JUMPING THE AI QUEUE

A local young man wanted to do a pilates class but it was booked out so he asked AI to do something and it got him a spot by dropping someone else off the list. A bit of luck, or AI hacking a system, or just a test run for our future masters? It sounds silly but so did planes, cars and probably trains at some stage.

The technology could go wrong, the basis of many movies, it could affect the share prices, for the few that can afford batches of shares, or it could help me. I could use it to get me better seats at a show, to adjust the traffic light sequences so I always get green, or a real achievement would be to get my numbers to be the lottery numbers but only once every month so it doesn’t look suspicious.

AI isn’t the real problem, it’s AI on the loose being used by a maniac with ‘a few screws loose up top’, in the same way that a gun isn’t dangerous, it’s the person holding the gun.

Make sure the ‘off’ switch is big and easy to access.

Dennis Fitzgerald,

28 Landale St,

Box Hill, Vic

Australia

World.title: WOMEN AND NIGERIA’S DAIRY ECONOMY
World.content:
When women prosper, the rural economies grow, contends GLORIA ANAJA AUDU

For generations, women have been central to Nigeria’s dairy economy, milking cattle at dawn, processing fresh milk into traditional products, selling in local markets, managing household nutrition, and reinvesting earnings into their families. Their contributions had never been in question. Yet many rural women have remained largely excluded from the formal financial systems that increasingly shape economic opportunity not for lack of ambition, but for lack of the financial tools to grow what they were already building. Nationally, an estimated 25 million Nigerian women remain formally unbanked, and 16 million rely exclusively on informal financial mechanisms. The gender gap in financial access has not been closing but widening, from roughly 10% in 2012 to 12% in 2020, with projections suggesting it will persist above 10% through 2027.

Financial inclusion matters not as an end in itself, but because it expands choice: a secure place to save and lets households plan beyond immediate needs. Formal services reduce dependence on costly or unreliable informal lending. Savings groups create room for collective investment; and financial records build credibility with banks, buyers and commercial partners. Together, these changes build economic agency, the ability to make decisions, manage resources, and pursue opportunity. Global evidence consistently links women’s control over financial resources to greater household investment in education, nutrition, healthcare and productive assets.

The Advancing Local Dairy Development in Nigeria (ALDDN) reflects this pattern. Rather than treating financial inclusion as a standalone activity, the programme embedded it in the daily life of farmer organizations. Self-help groups became more than savings mechanisms, they became spaces where women built financial confidence, exchanged knowledge, and developed relationships supporting both economic and social goals. A traditional ruler in Zaria, Kaduna State, put it simply during the programme’s closing research: for the first time, he said, women in his community were saving and accessing loans on their own account; his own wife no longer needed to come to him to fund the household kitchen. By programme close, more than 12,000 formal bank accounts had been opened and self-help groups had mobilized approximately ₦75 million in cumulative savings. Behind each figure sits a woman with greater financial security, a network of trust, and a household making decisions with more confidence.

As financial capability increased, the organizations themselves grew stronger: members participated more actively in decision-making, savings strengthened organizational sustainability, and leadership responsibilities broadened. Financial inclusion is often framed as a social intervention. The evidence here suggests it is equally an economic strategy, financially capable members strengthen collective action, and stronger collective action supports more efficient markets. “The most important outcome of financial inclusion is not a bank account. It is the confidence and capability to make economic decisions that shape the future.”

When women prosper, rural economies grow.

Development is often measured in indicators, accounts opened, savings accumulated, women in producer groups. These metrics matter, but the real significance lies in the decisions they make possible. A woman who saves consistently is better positioned to invest in her enterprise; a woman with access to financial services is better prepared to absorb a shock without selling livestock or cutting household consumption. Individually modest, these decisions accumulate into community-level change, which is why economists increasingly describe women’s economic participation as a multiplier rather than a single intervention.

Within ALDDN’s self-help groups and cooperatives, this played out through more than finance. Groups became spaces to exchange business ideas, discuss household investments, and solve shared problems, building social networks that proved as valuable as the savings themselves. Many groups organized their savings on two tracks at once: a credit and loan fund for productive investment, and a separate social welfare fund that members could draw on immediately, without paperwork or delay, in the event of illness, a birth, or a wedding. A self-help group leader in Rubwoi, Plateau State, described this second fund as the reason members stayed committed even in lean months, it meant the group could show up for a member in crisis the same day, something no bank in the area could do. As participation grew, many women also took on leadership: chairing meetings, managing savings records, coordinating activities, and representing members to processors and financial institutions. That shift matters because institutions perform better when leadership reflects the people they serve, broader participation strengthens accountability, and greater transparency builds trust.

This challenges a common framing: women’s economic participation is not a social add-on to agricultural development, but one of the mechanisms through which it succeeds. Stronger financial participation strengthens farmer organizations; stronger organizations make markets more reliable; more reliable markets give rural households the confidence to invest further a cycle that reinforces itself over time.

The Ripple Effect of Women’s Economic Agency:

Individual: increased savings, financial confidence, productive investment. Household: improved resilience, better financial planning, greater investment in wellbeing. Farmer organization: stronger leadership, better governance, increased participation. Market system: reliable supply, stronger institutions, inclusive growth.

Women’s economic agency generates value far beyond individual livelihoods — it strengthens the entire rural economy.

Agricultural development has traditionally centered on value chains, production, processing, market access, productivity. These remain fundamental, but experience increasingly shows technical interventions alone cannot deliver lasting transformation, because markets are ultimately shaped by people: the decisions producers make, the relationships they build, and the institutions through which they collaborate. This has driven a shift toward thinking about inclusive market systems, in which all actors are equipped to participate and benefit, a frame in which women’s economic agency is not a gender objective but a market systems imperative.

Within ALDDN, financial inclusion, self-help groups and cooperative participation were not run as isolated activities. As women became more financially capable, farmer organizations grew stronger; as organizations strengthened, relationships with processors became more reliable; as commercial relationships firmed up, confidence rose across the value chain. Investment at the household level generated improvements throughout the system.

This carries a practical design lesson. Gender interventions are too often built as parallel tracks, women’s training delivered separately, financial inclusion managed independently, leadership development treated as an add-on rather than core architecture. ALDDN’s experience argues for the opposite: a dairy value chain cannot become more competitive while half its economic actors remain constrained by limited access to finance, leadership, or commercial networks. Embedding women’s participation into the core design of a programme is not an inclusion requirement, it is a performance requirement, with the same logic applying well beyond dairy, to climate-smart agriculture, food security, and rural enterprise more broadly. “The question is no longer whether women should participate in agricultural markets. The question is whether agricultural markets can reach their full potential without women’s full economic participation.”

A credible account of this progress has to include where it fell short of target, and why. Bank account openings reached 12,299 against a goal of 15,750 — 78%. Formal credit linkage for women lagged further still: 1,706 women were connected to formal credit against a target of 3,150, or 54%. And only 7,045 female farmers had gone on to access two or more services from their cooperative, against a target of over 13,000 — roughly half, with distribution still ongoing at programme close.

These gaps are not evidence that the approach failed; they are evidence of where a six-year programme runs into constraints no single project can fully resolve on its own. Rural bank branch density in much of Northern Nigeria has not caught up to where these farmer groups actually operate, and while microfinance institutions are expanding into the area, they are doing so slowly. Roughly 40% of ALDDN’s cooperatives are less than two years old at programme close, the institutional muscle needed to negotiate formal credit or operate independently of programme support simply takes longer to build than a project cycle allows. And underneath both of those constraints sits a more basic one: documentation. Many women face structural barriers around national ID and bank verification number requirements, digital literacy, and social norms around independently managing money, barriers that sit upstream of any single group’s capability and require investment well beyond the dairy value chain.

The gender pattern shows up starkly in the underlying data: only 9% of women farmers in the programme had a mobile wallet or bank account, compared with 14% of men. In mixed-gender groups, women were disproportionately confined to secretarial roles even where they were active participants, while chairperson positions, the roles most likely to interface directly with a bank or a processor remained predominantly male. Financial inclusion, in other words, is not gender-neutral by default, even inside a programme explicitly designed to make it so.

None of this diminishes the ₦75 million in mobilized savings or the 12,299 accounts opened. If anything, it sharpens the more useful lesson underneath both numbers: informal, group-based savings outperformed target by a wide margin precisely because it required none of the documentation, infrastructure, or institutional maturity that formal credit and banking still demand. That is not a consolation prize. It is a sequencing lesson, build the savings habit and the trust it depends on first, and treat the transition to banks, digital payments and third-party credit as the next stage, not the first one.

Agricultural development has long been measured by what farmers produce, more milk, higher yields, greater market access. These outcomes remain important, but ALDDN’s experience suggests sustainable transformation is shaped by something deeper: who has the opportunity to participate fully in that growth. Women’s contribution to Northern Nigeria’s dairy economy was never in question. What changed through the programme was their ability to participate more fully in the economic systems surrounding it, through access to savings, financial services, organized producer groups, leadership, and markets.

As governments, private-sector actors, and development partners plan the next generation of agricultural investment, this deserves consideration alongside infrastructure, technology, and climate resilience. None of those investments reach full potential unless the people who sustain agricultural systems daily are equally equipped to participate in the opportunities they create. That means designing financial inclusion into the architecture of rural development rather than around its edges, with producer organizations that intentionally cultivate women’s leadership, and market systems that recognize women as entrepreneurs, producers, investors and leaders, not beneficiaries at the margins.

The story of ALDDN reaches beyond dairy. It suggests that investing in women’s economic agency does more than improve individual livelihoods, it strengthens the human systems that allow markets to function and local economies to adapt. Perhaps the more useful question for what comes next is not whether women should be included in agricultural development, but how much faster that development could move if their economic agency were treated as a core investment rather than a complementary one.

Audu is of ALDDN programme, implemented by Sahel Consulting Agriculture & Nutrition Limited in partnership with TechnoServe Nigeria with support from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation

World.title: THE PREVALENCE OF SEXUAL VIOLENCE
World.content:
All stakeholders must do more to protect our women

That violence continues to manifest itself in new forms and trends against women and girls in Nigeria is no longer a matter of conjecture. One in every five Nigerian women aged 15 to 49 has experienced physical or sexual violence, according to the latest statistics from the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP). The report emerged last Tuesday during their collaboration with the European Union (EU) and International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA) on how the media could be used to challenge institutional failures and break the culture of silence surrounding sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) in the country.

Despite the stringent provisions in the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act 2015, there is hardly a day without a report of a man visiting violence either on his spouse or girlfriend. The law prohibits, among others, abandonment of spouse, children and other dependents without sustenance, battery, and harmful traditional practices. It provides a legislative and legal framework for the prevention of all forms of violence against vulnerable persons, especially women and girls, and prohibits economic abuse, forced isolation and separation from family and friends.

We therefore endorse the initiative unveiled in Abuja under the EU-supported End Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Programme, with journalists receiving specialised training to investigate and report cases of sexual and gender-based violence more effectively, ethically, and sensitively. We cannot continue to ignore the societal upsurge in these occurrences, for the implications on our collective psyche, as citizenry, and our development as a nation.

From physical and verbal abuse to rape and even murder, it is evident that relevant authorities are not doing enough to tackle this menace. While spousal abuse indeed cuts across both sexes, women are predominantly the victims in the country. Yet abused women rarely report the violence they endure, for fear of being stigmatised by the society. Besides, the patriarchal interpretations within our various faiths preach endurance. This has largely led to the current climate of impunity.

Against the background that curbing these tragic incidents is a collective responsibility, both the authorities and the society must be alerted to the fact that battery and assault remain felonies in our law books, even where inflicted between spouses. We also understand that ignoring the subtle signals of violence can only lead to fatal consequences as we have witnessed lately. To worsen matters, assault and battery, even though serious offences, are hardly ever perceived as crimes by many of our law enforcement agencies, unless the acts ultimately culminate in the occurrence of death.

It is therefore imperative that all relevant stakeholders make more efforts to understand the underlying causes and dynamics of this growing violence, if only to redeem the stability of the family unit, and the larger society. But for this initiative to achieve the desired results, it should expand its orbit beyond the media. It is, for instance, a notorious fact that even when complaints of violence and abuse (against family members) are made at our police stations—where girls and women can summon the courage to do so—they are often dismissed as domestic matters, especially where such violence occurs between spouses.

We need the collaboration between the media, security agencies and government, at all levels, to effectively address these concerns. That is the only way to assure our women and girls that we care about their welfare and wellbeing, and the health and prosperity of Nigeria.

World.title: THE PROPOSED OPPOSITION CONSENSUS CANDIDACY
World.content:
MONDAY PHILIPS EKPE writes that rival candidates in next year’s presidential poll do not stand much chance outside coalition

For now, it appears like kite-flying. The August 2, 2026 open letter conceived and signed by the self-styled G100 will need to be backed soon by stronger energies and actions in order to pass the test of a true catalyst for any consequential political engineering in the runup to the 2027 presidential election. The group had given itself two weeks to bring together the leading lights of the opposition political parties in order to kickstart the process of unifying them towards presenting a single candidate to challenge the incumbent president. The members didn’t seem to consider the conflict with the Osun State governorship poll this weekend.

But the awkward announced timing shouldn’t take any shine off the validity and urgency of this proposition. The group’s front-liners like former National Vice Chairman of All Progressives Congress (North-West), Malam Salihu Lukman, former member of the House of Representatives, Honourable Nnenna Ukeje, ex-Deputy Governor of Kogi State, Chief Simon Achuba, and political economist and public intellectual, Professor Anthony Kila, must be sufficiently conversant with the centrality of virile opposition to the integrity of any democracy and, by implication, every election cycle. Ordinarily, the summit they’re planning with their 96 colleagues should be embraced by all lovers of inclusive, collaborative democratic practice.

As altruistic as their mission is, whether it’ll come to fruition remains to be seen. The G100’s initial statement titled, “The Doctrine of a Necessary Democratic Opposition”, reads thus, in part: “We have fashioned a political order that too often rewards loyalty over merit, patronage over service, and power over accountability. We should not wonder that such a system produces poverty and misery; for, a nation cannot harvest prosperity from institutions that perpetuate poverty and deprivation.

“The ruling party grows stronger, not only because of its own organisation, but because it has surrendered internal dissent to the authority of the executive. At the same time, those entrusted with presenting Nigerians with an alternative have become divided by ambition rather than united by purpose. While the executive consolidates power, the opposition fragments…. The liberty of a people depends not only upon the existence of government, but upon the certainty that government may be peacefully challenged, corrected and, when necessary, replaced. A government that fears no opposition soon forgets the people. An opposition that cannot oppose soon forgets its purpose.

“Nigeria cannot be rescued by opposition leaders who march separately toward the same defeat. Personal ambition must submit to national necessity, for a people divided at the moment of decision will remain governed by those who profit from that division….” A well-crafted epistle which could turn out to be historic or prophetic. Or, perhaps, be remembered only for its poetic qualities – something even enemies of Nigeria shouldn’t wish this underperforming giant of Africa and a potentially bold and respected global player.

The country, no doubt, is at a crossroads, a delicate phase of nation-building and growth. A point where the slide on the graph of decent and progressive human development is yet to show appreciable signs of going upwards. It won’t be correct to lay all the blames for the nation’s current misfortune at the doorsteps of President Bola Tinubu and his government since the origin of most of the challenges does not, in truth, belong to the present. Sadly, though, Nigerians are now saddled with the wisdom or unwisdom of investing so much confidence in Tinubu’s ability to deliver the good life, especially against the backdrop of succeeding a lacklustre President Muhammadu Buhari administration.

Attribute it to nostalgia, short memory, mischief, ignorance, sincere testimony, or jejune politics, for all you want. Many people today think that their lives were much better during Buhari’s time than now, as painful as it was. Tinubu’s official and self-appointed image minders won’t mind losing a limb in defence of their master’s intentions, reforms and programmes. Not surprisingly. But one thing, in God’s name, they mustn’t do is to view the quest for a strong political rivalry as an unpatriotic, evil gang-up. So much has been said about Tinubu’s combative role in the processes that led to the unseating of President Goodluck Jonathan in 2015. If he hadn’t done so, together with his aggressive, relentless co-travellers, the then overfed ruling party, People’s Democratic Party (PDP), would still be running the show today. And now that many Nigerian citizens feel much the same towards this government, erecting a viable platform that would project a viable alternative is a most patriotic thing to do.

Ironically, the president may not even be the greatest worry at this point. One immediate hurdle is for Malam Lukman and Co to get the heavyweight targets of this move to first attend the parley and then show respect to its ideals. It’s instructive that the highest losers in the 2023 presidential election are in this mix: Wazirin Atiku Abubakar, now presidential candidate of African Democratic Congress (ADC), Mr Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and his running mate, Dr Rabiu Kwankwaso; among other political titans.

These men can serve their country and themselves creditably if they dwell less on their own past records, particularly the rankings of the last outing. Reason: Times have changed remarkably. So have attitudes. The figures that were recorded in their favour by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) – whatever veracity is left of them – may have lost their relevance. Any permutations based on those numbers now may actually be in futility. For instance, I’ve met many young people who are so disappointed by Obi’s loss that they’ve lost faith in the country’s electoral system altogether. And, quite frankly, it’ll take more than simply hammering of the people’s unending suffering to turn the tide.

Getting apathetic individuals and sections to participate this time would be a function of several variables, one of which is the readiness of the front bench players to sacrifice their own ambitions – not minding legitimacy and expediency – for the general good. The ever-increasing incidence of voter indifference validates this. By now, the presidential frontrunners might have learnt some critical lessons. One simple arithmetic of the 2023 outing is that if Abubakar and Obi had run on the same ticket, nothing would have given Tinubu the victory, as demonstrated by the declared results. Now that the beneficiary of that costly calculation is in power, no soothsayer is required to declare that it’ll take extraordinary efforts (in this case, a well-mobilised coalition) to remove him. Anything short of that would be sleep-walking into a certain trouncing.

Dr Ekpe is a member of THISDAY Editorial Board

X: @monday_ekpe2

World.title: PASSPORTS AND THE PECKING ORDER
World.content:
Your passport dictates how you are treated. But it can be reversed, argues JOSHUA J. OMOJUWA

Take two men and a plane ticket. The first is an American or a Canadian who, some years ago, served time in prison. A convicted felon. Yet if he wakes tomorrow and decides to holiday in Rome, the only thing between him and the trip is a booking website. No embassy asks him to explain himself. No official weighs his worthiness. His passport does the vouching.

The second man is Aliko Dangote, or Abdulsamad Rabiu, or any Nigerian of comparable standing you care to name. Before either of them can even think about that same Roman holiday, the first question is whether a Schengen visa already sits in the Nigerian passport. If it does not, the holiday becomes a project. Weeks must be set aside. A small mountain of documents must be assembled: bank statements, letters of employment or, in their case, proof of empire, hotel reservations, return tickets, insurance, an itinerary, all to persuade a consular officer that these men can be trusted to enter Europe and, above all, to leave it again. Africa’s most accomplished industrialists must audition for a permission a felon from Ohio never has to seek.

I have used Europe as the illustration, but do not mistake the example for the rule. The same wall stands around almost the entire world. Swap Rome for New York, London, Johannesburg, Ottawa, Tokyo or Canberra and the story barely changes. Swap Dangote for a doctor from Dhaka, an engineer from Nairobi, a lawyer from Lima or a teacher from Manila, and it does not change at all. This is not a Nigerian grievance. It is the shared condition of most of the global south, where the citizen of a poor country must negotiate a gauntlet of visas, fees, interviews and suspicion to enter a rich one, while the citizen of a rich country crosses the earth on a booklet and a booking. The irony is that countries of the global south have mimicked these walls against themselves whilst throwing their gates open for those who defined the norm. A double tragedy.

This tells you how the world is actually organised. The felon and the billionaire are not judged on their lives. They are judged on their origin: where you were born, and what that birthplace is presumed to be worth.

The world was built by those with the tools to set the rules, and they set them to restrict the ordinary citizen of the global south. The rules do not distinguish between us. They group us. They flatten the professor and the fraudster, the surgeon and the stowaway, into one suspect category defined by the cover of a booklet. Your life’s work does not matter. Only your nationality does, and it has already been scored, filed, and, in most consular back offices, quietly treated as a flight risk.

We can recite the Universal Declaration of Human Rights until we are hoarse. It says everyone has the right to leave any country and return to his own. A beautiful sentence, and for the holder of a Nigerian, Kenyan, Bangladeshi or Bolivian passport, largely theoretical, because the right to leave your country means little when no other is obliged to let you in, and the ones you most want to visit assume you plan to overstay. Whatever the declarations say on paper, one thing is clear in practice. These countries do not rate us, and a passport is only a nation’s promise about its people. To distrust the document is to distrust the citizen.

The same nations that lecture us about openness have made themselves the most closed places on earth for people who look like us. That is true, and none of it changes a single visa decision. The consular officer is not moved by our sense of injustice. The gap in mobility is not an argument we win by being right about it. It is a gap in power, and gaps in power do not close because you complain about them. They close when you build power that makes them impossible to sustain.

So the useful question is not how dare they. It is what this teaches us about where we stand. The passports that open doors belong to countries the world needs, whose economies, institutions and citizens others cannot do without. It goes to nations too productive, too stable and too important to be waved into the queue. The strength of your passport is a scoreboard of your country’s power, and we read our own low score every time we assemble those documents.

Most of the work is work at home. A Nigeria, or any southern nation, whose institutions worked, whose economy grew year on year, whose citizens were plainly building rather than fleeing, would in time change the assumption that governs those consular desks. Visa-free travel tracks almost exactly with prosperity and good governance.

If the global north has decided to group us together whatever our merit, let us take that same logic of grouping and turn it to our own use. An African passport that lets an African move freely across Africa? A market big enough that our own continent is worth staying in? Regional institutions that make our movement our own decision rather than another capital’s favour? These we have the power to build. We cannot legislate our way into the north’s good opinion. We can build homes so worth living in that its opinion matters less every year.

The ticket the felon buys without a second thought is a free lesson, and the lesson is simple. The world respects power and prices everything else. The answer is not to protest the ranking but to change the numbers. That work is slow, unglamorous, the work of a generation, and it is entirely ours. It starts with seeing the order for what it is and refusing to accept that our place in it is fixed forever. One study by the LAGO Collective puts the loss to applicants from developing regions at157 million euros per year on rejected, non-refundable short-term Schengen (EU) visas. Reverse remittances. Tragic.

Omojuwa is chief strategist, Alpha Reach/BGX Publishing

World.title: AmaZulu striker apologises to injured Orlando Pirates midfielder
World.content:
AmaZulu striker Thandolwenkosi Ngwenya has issued an apology to the injured Orlando Pirates midfielder Sihle Nduli.

On Wednesday night, the Buccaneers visited Usuthu in the two teams’ second league matches of the season.

The game ended in a 1-1 draw with Tshepang Moremi opening the scoring for Pirates before Ngwenya equalised for AmaZulu on the stroke of half-time.



Also read: Orlando Pirates midfielder suffers another injury blow on return

AMAZULU STRIKER NGWENYA APOLOGISES TO ORLANDO PIRATES MIDFIELDER NDULI

Now, in the second half of the same game, in the 53rd minute to be precise, Ngwenya stamped onto Nduli and injured him.

The incident saw Nduli being stretchered off the pitch as he could not continue with the game after that horrific injury.



What’s more painful for Nduli and the rest of the Pirates team is that the 30-year-old midfielder had just returned from a long injury layoff.

The former Stellenbosch FC anchorman had been out since November 2025 with an Achilles tendon injury he suffered against Golden Arrows.

Also read: Orlando Pirates drop points away to AmaZulu



NGWENYA’S APOLOGY TO NDULI

“I’m sorry my brother for what happened,” wrote Ngwenya on his Instagram account.

“I did not do it intentionally. [I] hope you got space in your heart to forgive me. Speedy recovery,” he concluded.

World.title: How MUCH is Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot?
World.content:
Check out the lay of the land for the Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot. Will you be in the running? Image: File

How much is the Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot on 15 August worth? Well, it breaks down like so: Straight Lotto will be worth R13 million, Lotto Plus 1 sits at R1.5 million and, for Lotto Plus Max 5, you can tag on another R3.5 million. All tallied up, that puts the total worth at R18 million for Saturday. That’s an increase of R3 million across all three games after a full quota of rollovers this week …

As ever, success for Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot on 15 August 2026 comes from knowing how recently one of the three has just paid out big. This is the first game in a while that benefits from rollovers across the board. Previously, small resets across any one of the three games were tempering winnings. Payouts, while more frequent, are rarely climbing high though …

SATURDAY LOTTO AND LOTTO PLUS JACKPOT 15 AUGUST 2026

As such, the Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot on 15 August is more like Sizekhaya’s bread-and-butter game. Cheaper than PowerBall and PowerBall XTRA, much easier to win, but less dramatic in jackpot size. Nevertheless, Sizekhaya’s 1 June 2026 takeover reshaped it even further. The core mechanics require players to choose six numbers from a pool of 1 to 52, which is reduced from 1 to 58 previously.



As ever, numbers can be chosen manually or auto generated through the popular Quick Pick. Pricing sits lower than PowerBall’s increase. A standard Lotto board costs R5, with Lotto Plus 1 adding R2.50 and Lotto 5 Max adding a further R2.50 on top. Therefore, playing all three together costs R10 per board.

What players are still wrapping their head around is the new MultiPlay (MP1) option. It lets players add a seventh number to their existing six in each of the three games. And it gets proportionally more expensive as you go. The total combination if you add MP1 across all boards is R70 – that’s R35 + R17.50 + R17.50. However, your odds are massively improved if you do go down this rabbit hole.

HOW TO HANDLE MULTIPLAY

Would you prefer small and often, or one time and massive? This is the difference between Lotto and PowerBall. Image: File

If you add MP1 to Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot across all three games, your total ticket will cost R70.00. Plus, if you’re using your banking app, be sure to lookout for digital banking fee of roughly R2.95 added to the transaction. So, the question remains, is it worth spending the extra money? Jackpot odds have already improved substantially under the new number matrix. The chances of matching all six numbers now sits at 1 in 20 million.



That’s twice as likely as the old 1 in 40 million under ITHUBA. However, dabble with the MP1 and all of a sudden, you’re playing with seven numbers instead of six. This means your odds now become just 1 in 2.9 million, which represents a straight sevenfold improvement. And don’t forget that’s across all three games since they share the board.

DRAW TIMES AND CLAIMING WINNINGS

Remember, if you’re playing Saturday Lotto and Lotto Plus jackpot, decide on a budget before buying lotto tickets, and don’t chase a bad week by spending more. The National Responsible Gambling Programme runs a toll-free counselling line on 0800 006 008 for anyone who is struggling.

Lotto and Lotto Plus draws twice weekly at 21:00. Sizekhaya brought back live televised draws using physical draw machines. Ticket sales cut off half an hour before the draw typically at 20:30. All lottery prizes must be claimed within 365 days of the draw date. Anyone who misses that window forfeits their prize and the money is transferred to the National Lottery Distribution Trust for charitable causes.

World.title: 7 Salaries: Former Orlando Pirates midfielder reveals all payments
World.content:
Morton shared his base salaries from Orlando Pirates, Maritzburg United, SuperSport United, AmaZulu, Cape Moya, Cape All Stars and Cape Town Spurs.

MICHAEL MORTON STARTED ON R20,000 AT ORLANDO PIRATES

Morton began his professional career at Orlando Pirates during the 2008/09 season. At just 19, he signed a three-year deal worth R20,000 per month.

“Nobody in South African football has ever done this before. I’m about to show you every single contract I signed in my 17 years as a professional footballer,” Morton said on X.



He said the salary changed his life. “That money really set me up nicely,” Morton explained. He used it to buy his first apartment and a used Peugeot 206 for R60,000 cash.

After loan spells at Wits, Morton joined Maritzburg United in 2010. His salary increased to the R30,000 range. He then signed a pre-contract with SuperSport United. His monthly salary jumped into the R60,000 range.

Morton’s biggest payday followed his move to AmaZulu. He revealed that he earned in the R80,000 range, making it the most lucrative contract of his career.



“This was actually my most lucrative contract of my career,” he said.

COVID-19 FORCED MORTON TO TAKE A CUT

The COVID-19 pandemic hit just as Morton became a free agent. He eventually joined Cape Moya in the NFD. His salary dropped from the R80,000 range to R30,000.

Also read: Transfer news: Orlando Pirates sign Dublin Boon



Morton described it as a 67% pay cut. “That was a bit of a shock going from the highest I was earning in my career back to square one,” he said.

He then earned R30,000 at Cape All Stars before joining Cape Town Spurs on the same salary. However, Morton negotiated a promotion clause. When Cape Town Spurs won promotion, his salary doubled from R30,000 to R60,000.

The club immediately returned to the NFD after relegation. Morton’s salary dropped back to R30,000. He played a few more matches before retiring.



Morton stressed that his figures cover base salaries only. They exclude bonuses, signing-on fees and image rights.

“These are pretty accurate estimates, not done to the exact Rand,” he said. “It’ll give you a pretty good idea of what I earned over the course of my career,” he said.

World.title: Gayton McKenzie opens up about his sick son: ‘Prepare for the worst’
World.content:
Gayton McKenzie has opened up about his son's medical issues. Images via Facebook

Gayton McKenzie has opened up his battle with a chronically ill child, who he believes was miraculously healed by answered prayer.

The Minister of Sport, Art and Culture shared the personal account in a heartfelt social media post.

GAYTON MCKENZIE SHARES POST ABOUT SICK SON

On his Facebook account, Gayton McKenzie shared a post about one of his sons, Cruz McKenzie.



The Minister and Patriotic Alliance leader shared: “This boy had so many things wrong with him medically when he was born, he was rushed to the ICU and kept there for a long time.

“We literally lived at the hospital. The doctors called me one side and said I should prepare my family for the worst.

Gayton added that his mother encouraged the family to continue praying and to ignore the doctor’s reports.

He continued: “We would pray without stopping. He was discharged and healed fully. He has never gotten sick or needed medical care again. He is a very bright teenager today, he once told me that he can get hundred percent in a test and he did it. He is a great soccer player today and such a joy.

Gayton shared that the motive for the post was to encourage parents who are going through similar circumstances.

“Prayer works, it is a joke for those that has not experience the result of prayer. Some of us fortunate enough to have experienced the power of prayer can testify from rooftops about the wonders of serving a Living and Loving God”, he added.



HOW MANY CHILDREN DOES HE HAVE?

In an interview on Morning Live in 2015, Gayton McKenzie stated that at the time, he had eight children with six women.

The PA party leader was speaking about his book titled The Uncomfortable Truth.

The memoir was written from the former convict’s experiences with love, casual sex, and relationships.

“I’ve got eight kids with six different women. Those were in my player days…in my very naughty days”, he told a surprised Leanne.

However, he added that despite the unconventional dynamic, he was not an absent father.

“Their surnames are all McKenzie; I look after all my kids.”

Gayton has remained mum about the identities of the six women who bore his eight children, one of whom is Siwelele FC owner Calvin Le John.

However, it is public knowledge that he wed his lawyer, Nicolette Joubert, in 2003.

This came after Nicolette was sent to investigate Gayton and others’ allegations of corruption at the Grootvlei Prison involving prison gangs, warders, and inmates. The exposé became international news, and Gayton was named one of the “Grootvlei Four.”

The couple had two daughters together.

A decade later, Gayton hinted that he had wronged his wife, whom he had since divorced.

He tweeted: “I hurt my ex-wife indescribably. But a bad word about me will never be heard by strangers or our kids, sheer class always.”

World.title: ‘We fear no one’ – Kaizer Chiefs star fires warning at Sundowns
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs defender Miguel Inacio has sent a strong warning to Mamelodi Sundowns ahead of their blockbuster Betway Premiership clash at FNB Stadium on Saturday.

Amakhosi have made an impressive start to the league campaign, winning their opening two matches and building early momentum under coach Fernando Da Cruz.

Inacio, who has been a key figure in Chiefs’ defence, insists his side will not be intimidated by the reigning champions.



“We have to respect the fact that Sundowns is Sundowns, but we are also Kaizer Chiefs and we fight for our goals. We fear no one,” Inacio said.

“I think the message is clear: we fear no one, no matter if they are champions of Africa or champions of the PSL. We are going to start the game with the same ambition and fighting spirit, and win every duel.”

will also take confidence from their recent record against Sundowns, having avoided defeat in their last three meetings across all competitions.



Kaizer Chiefs ready for Sundowns

For Inacio, Saturday’s encounter also presents an opportunity to continue his strong start to the season and potentially catch the attention of the Angola national team selectors.

The defender has been out of the national team setup for several years but admits a return to the Palancas Negras is something he would welcome.

“I won’t lie, I would like to make it back to the national team, but my focus right now is Kaizer Chiefs and achieving goals with my club,” he said during a press conference at the Chiefs Village on Thursday afternoon.



“We have a lot of games and competitions ahead of us. I never think about the national team ahead of any game. The only thing on my mind right now is Leon, Tashreeq and all the Sundowns attack.

“So, that is all that I am thinking about, which is the next game for us and obviously remaining fit, training well and being prepared to be one of the options for coach Da Cruz against Sundowns.”

When do Kaizer Chiefs play Sundowns?

Kaizer Chiefs host Mamelodi Sundowns at FNB Stadium on Saturday, 15 August, with kick-off scheduled for 15:00.



The highly anticipated encounter will be televised live on SABC 1 and SuperSport 2.

World.title: SASSA payment delays leave pensioners facing lapsed policies
World.content:
Reader reaction to The South African’s report on shifting SASSA payment dates has revealed just how far the disruption reaches, touching insurance, rent, and even other grant types.

Commenter Masters Jacob shared a blunt update: their AVBOB policy has already lapsed. Funeral policies like these are a common financial priority for pensioners, often built up over years of careful payments. Also, a lapse can mean losing that cover entirely or having to restart contributions from zero, a serious blow for recipients with little room in their budgets to absorb the loss.

Rent penalties add pressure

The financial strain isn’t limited to insurance. Commenter Jaap Loggenberg detailed a direct cost tied to payment timing, noting an extra R270 charge on rent for paying after the 2nd of the month, a penalty that eats into a grant many already describe as insufficient to live on.



Furthermore, not all the fallout is directly linked to payment dates. Commenter Alvenita Calvert reported that they still have not received their child support grant, suggesting the disruption may extend beyond the Older Persons Grant to other forms of SASSA assistance.

Taken together, the comments paint a picture of a support system under strain, one where delays and shifting schedules are creating financial consequences recipients never signed up for. Also, for pensioners and grant recipients already stretched thin, the message is consistent: even small administrative changes can carry outsized costs for those with the least room to absorb them.
