World.title: WestJet agrees to pay settlement in sexual harassment suit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet has agreed to pay $4.5 million to settle a sexual harassment class-action lawsuit launched a decade ago involving more than 3,000 flight attendants, according to the lead plaintiff and her lawyer.

They say a B.C. judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalized in June. WestJet said in a statement it is "pleased" to have reached a settlement.

Former flight attendant Mandalena Lewis alleged that a pilot sexually assaulted her on a layover in Hawaii in 2010. After launching a lawsuit in 2016, other women who worked for the airline came forward and the case was certified as a class action by the B.C. Court of Appeal in 2022.

The flight attendants allege WestJet failed to provide a safe workplace with adequate anti-harassment measures.

Lewis told CBC News on Wednesday she is relieved the case is done with, but doesn't feel like the plaintiffs got "full justice." She said she is feeling deflated by the "symbolic" dollar amount and the fact that WestJet did not admit wrongdoing under the terms of the agreement.

"It's the best we could get given the circumstances. I had to fight tooth and nail for these slivers," Lewis said.

The $4.5 million will be distributed among 3,452 flight attendants after expenses are deducted, including legal fees.

She said that works out to about $400 for each flight attendant involved in the suit.

Lewis says the judge also reduced her honorarium that was agreed to be paid out in the settlement, to $10,000 from $20,000.

"At the end of the day, I'm glad this is over, I am glad we set a legal precedent. I'm not glad with the number, I don't think it's enough."

Mandalena Lewis in a video interview with CBC News Wednesday. Lewis says she is relieved the legal process is over, but doesn't feel the plaintiffs got 'full justice.' (CBC News)

WestJet said in an email to CBC News it is "committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and well-being of all WestJetters" and "focused on advancing a culture of empowerment."

Under the terms of the settlement, WestJet is to retain a third-party consultant to conduct a workplace assessment to determine the prevalence of harassment in the workplace, the extent of underreporting and how to make reporting and response systems more effective.

Legal process a 'nightmare': Lewis

In an affidavit, Lewis said speaking with and supporting more than 100 former flight attendants regarding their experiences with sexual harassment — conversations she had in her role as lead plaintiff — took an extreme physical and emotional toll throughout the legal process.

She told CBC News on Wednesday that the experience has been a "nightmare."

Lewis said the sexual assault and harassment of female flight attendants is a "deep-seated, historical, systemic issue" that continues in the airline industry today.

"I took it on because I knew what a huge problem it was," she said. "I did it for myself and I did for other flight attendants who I know went through what I went through. And many are still going through it."

Lewis has said she reported the alleged 2010 assault to her managers and to the RCMP, who contacted police in Maui at the time. The U.S. federal prosecutor in Maui laid charges, but Lewis said she was told the pilot could only be arrested if he returned to the island.

Later, another flight attendant reached out to Lewis and alleged that she had been sexually assaulted by the same pilot in 2008.

In 2016, the airline fired Lewis for insubordination after she had demanded for months to see her employment record to determine whether WestJet took any action on her complaint.

The class-action suit settled Monday alleged that WestJet “breached contracts of employment with female flight attendants by failing to implement and maintain an adequate anti-harassment program, including adequate systems and practices for reporting, investigating, and responding to workplace harassment” between April 4, 2016 and Feb. 28, 2021.

WestJet denied those allegations.

The basis for compensation was costs that WestJet allegedly avoided through its failure to implement an adequate anti-harassment program, rather than compensation for harms suffered by the flight attendants.

Good deal for WestJet: lawyer

Joshua Coratti, associate lawyer with the Toronto employment law firm Ball Professional Corporation, says the settlement looks like a "pretty good deal" for WestJet, as it absolves them of liability for individual claims from plaintiffs, which could have been more costly.

"Doing a class-action lawsuit, you often end up with a lot less in terms of the monetary value for each individual plaintiff. As it turns out, typically lawyers are the ones who win the class action lawsuits. They're the ones collecting very large legal fees," Coratti told CBC News.

"What it can do, is it can show that certain behaviour is not permitted. It can get companies to be a little bit more hesitant to engage in large-scale violations to that effect."

World.title: 'Stuff happens': Doug Ford says he was unaware party allegedly followed former Liberal leader to Jamaica
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was unaware until Wednesday of his Progressive Conservative Party spending money to allegedly surveil former Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie in Jamaica in 2023.

The Trillium and POLICORNER reported on Thursday that the provincial party allegedly spent nearly $3,000 in donor and taxpayer dollars on two five-star resorts in Jamaica "to spy on" Bonnie Crombie as part of opposition research work. The story cited the claims to anonymous sources familiar with the plan.

The alleged surveillance took place six days after Crombie won the Liberal leadership in December 2023, when she was on a three-day vacation in Jamaica, The Trillium and POLICORNER reported.

CBC News has not independently confirmed The Trillium and POLICORNER's reporting.

However, in a statement on Thursday, the Ontario PC Party said: "The Ontario PC Party, like other political parties, conducts opposition research. In this instance, that work included travel to Jamaica in December 2023."

Ford said at an unrelated news conference Thursday that he does not approve of the alleged spying and he spoke to the party after hearing the claims Wednesday.

Ford said it was party money spent on the expense. Political parties in Ontario receive a per-vote subsidy, so party budgets are partly made up of taxpayer money.

"Things happen" in politics, Ford said, adding the trip was "no different" than when members of the media follow him on trips to the U.S.

Former Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie did not comment on the allegations, but did confirm that she vacationed in Jamaica in December 2023 and that she stayed at one of the hotels listed in the PC party's 2023 financial statement. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

When asked if being unaware of the incident absolves him of any blame, Ford said he relies on his team to make sure money is being spent appropriately.

"I don't watch every single dollar when I'm in the middle of a campaign," he said.

Ford was also asked if these tactics would continue, to which he replied, "I hope not."

"Let's just have fair and balanced elections," he said. "Stuff happens during elections."

Crombie said she is not commenting at this time, but confirmed to CBC News that she did take a vacation in Jamaica after the leadership race in 2023 and stayed at the Ocean Eden Bay resort.

CBC News obtained a copy of the PC Party's 2023 annual financial statement from the NDP. It showed office and administration expenses of $1,000.05 at the Ocean Eden Bay and $1,971.67 at the Royalton Negril Hotel, another resort in Jamaica.

The statement did not have information on when these expenses were incurred, for how long, or who claimed them. There are also no details on what the spending at the Royalton Negril Hotel was for.

'Heads need to roll': opposition party leaders

In a post on social media platform X, NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the alleged spying is "disgusting" and that Ford should not be allowed to "shrug it off."

"Spying on a woman who is one of your political opponents on her private vacation is creepy Trump-style politics that has no place here," she said.

Stiles said someone within the party had to sign off on the expense and that Ford will know exactly who it is.

"Heads need to roll," she said.

John Fraser, interim Leader of the Ontario Liberals, called on Ford to explain why someone was allegedly sent to follow Crombie to Jamaica and who exactly was involved.

"This isn't politics. This is creepy, disturbing behaviour and a complete abuse of power," said Fraser.

He said it was "extraordinary abuse of public money" to use donor and taxpayer funds to follow an opponent.

"It raises serious questions about how far Doug Ford is willing to go to target his political opponents, and whether this has happened before."

World.title: B.C. RCMP commanding officer relieved of duties following unspecified allegations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The RCMP's commanding officer in B.C. has been relieved of his duties following unspecified allegations dating from 2016 to 2018, according to a statement from the force.

Dwayne McDonald has been replaced in his capacity as deputy commissioner and B.C. RCMP commanding officer by John Brewer, who previously headed up B.C.'s extortion task force.

The statement, attributed to RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme on Thursday, said the force would not be providing further details on the allegations at this time.

"I want to reassure you that there will be no impact on RCMP operations or policing services in the province," Duheme said in the statement.

The statement says the allegations are under investigation.

McDonald was formerly the top cop at the Surrey RCMP, and served as the RCMP's criminal operations officer in charge of federal and organized crime investigations for the province of B.C.

CBC News has reached out to the RCMP for more on this story.

World.title: Guacamoles and salsas linked to U.S. jalapeño salmonella outbreak recalled in Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) has issued a recall of some Whole Foods Market brand products, saying they've been linked to a salmonella outbreak in the U.S.

Various guacamoles, pico de gallos, salsas and prepared foods it says were distributed in Ontario stores and online are part of the 22-item recall list issued Thursday.

CFIA says there have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products in Canada, but urges anyone who thinks they may have become sick from consuming a recalled product to contact their health-care provider.

More than 300 cases in U.S.

The agency says the recall is associated with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) investigation of salmonella illnesses related to jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.

The FDA says at least 345 people have fallen ill across the U.S. Officials say 36 hospitalizations are linked to the outbreak, with no recorded deaths.

A Public Health Agency of Canada spokesperson told CBC News in an email that the agency continually monitors outbreaks of enteric illnesses such as salmonella, and it is not currently investigating any salmonella illnesses associated with the U.S. outbreak.

A CFIA spokesperson told CBC News in an email last Thursday that, "at this time, there is no evidence that products implicated in this outbreak were distributed in Canada."

Food may not look or smell spoiled: CFIA

Salmonella is a type of bacteria that makes people sick with salmonellosis, an intestinal tract infection.

People most frequently get salmonella infections by ingesting food or water contaminated with feces that contains salmonella bacteria.

CFIA says food contaminated with salmonella may not look or smell spoiled, but can still make you sick.

Healthy people may experience fever, headache, vomiting, nausea, abdominal cramps and diarrhea, while young children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems may contract serious and potentially deadly infections, according to CFIA.

People usually begin to exhibit symptoms between six hours and six days after they are infected, and the symptoms can last between four to seven days, according to the CDC.

World.title: Private clinic Grifols says it's pausing all plasma collection in Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A for-profit plasma donation company says it's temporarily shutting down collection at all its Canadian clinics amid public scrutiny.

Grifols says it's pausing activities in light of "unfounded attention" focused on paid plasma collection and that it's ready to resume operations as soon as it's practicable, in agreement with Health Canada and the Canadian Blood Services.

Grifols said it informed Health Canada of its decision Wednesday, the same day the federal agency says the company was issued a non-compliance rating at one of its Winnipeg sites, on Taylor Avenue.

The company said the temporary pause will go into effect Friday.

An inspection report card summary on Health Canada's website Thursday said the clinic "did not carry out sufficient corrective and preventive actions when required."

It also said some operating procedures were not always followed and that records of "staff qualifications, training or evaluation of their competency" were not always sufficient.

Advocates have been calling on the federal government to crack down on the company after CBC News reported two people died after donating plasma at different Grifols clinics in Winnipeg.

A Health Canada inspection recently released under access to information laws found multiple issues with donor screening and supervision. Data from the federal agency show a total of 25 serious adverse reactions had been reported at centres currently operated by Grifols since 2018.

Health Canada had imposed conditions on more than a dozen sites operating under the Grifols licence.

The agency has ordered the company to reduce the number of donation appointments, reassess the number of trained workers in all positions, review donor files before updating eligibility and implement more oversight for newer staff, including in-person supervision.

This is on top of mandatory audits to make sure "that any deficiencies identified are documented and investigated."

Grifols said in a statement Thursday donor safety and the quality of the plasma it collects have never been compromised.

Winnipeg clinic found non-compliant

Publicly listed inspections of licensed blood establishments show the company's clinics have received "non-compliant" ratings in New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Most recently, a June 23 inspection of the Grifols location on Winnipeg's Taylor Avenue found problems in how the clinic screened donors for suitability, cleaned and maintained equipment and investigated errors and accidents, among other issues.

International student Rodiyat Alebede died on Oct. 25 after friends say she went to give plasma at the Taylor Avenue centre. Health Canada has said it's found no link between the 22-year-old’s death and the "donation process."

The Grifols location at 693 Taylor Ave. in Winnipeg. A Health Canada inspection in June found several deficiencies there. (CBC)

A spokesperson for Health Minister Marjorie Michel said in a statement Thursday that Health Canada had been working closely with the company to address deficiencies before taking "additional remedial measures."

The measures included extra terms and conditions to Grifol's licence, an unannounced inspection and a formal warning saying the identified problems could result in suspension of some operations, the statement said.

"Canadians' safety must always come first, and we welcome Grifols' decision to temporarily close its plasma collection sites across Canada," the minister's office said after the company announced the temporary closure, adding it won't impact the country's blood supply.



Grifols said the pause will allow the company to work with the government and Canadian Blood Services on a plasma collection network "without unnecessary reliance on imported product."

The Spain-based company has about 400 plasma collection centres outside Canada.

World.title: U.S. can maintain 'indefinite' naval blockade of Iran if needed, Hegseth says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The United States on Thursday threatened to maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely, ratcheting up economic pressure on Tehran as ceasefire talks have floundered, global oil supply ‌is dropping and regional tensions are rising.

U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that the U.S. military could keep a naval presence in the region to enforce its blockade of Iran, which has inflicted severe economic damage on the country.

"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Hegseth ​told reporters on a trip to Panama.

With a tentative June deal to end ​the war in tatters, Iran has sought to control the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked some vessels trying to transit the strategic waterway, through which a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas travelled before the war ​began in February.

Two vessels from the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked transiting the strait on ⁠Thursday evening, UAE state news agency WAM ⁠reported. The United Arab Emirates government condemned it as an Iranian attack.

Shipping ‌traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels on Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels, and 130 to 140 ships before the war.

Iran rejects Trump's claim of control

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted that the U.S. has "total control" over the strait.

Iran said in an X post that those claims "do not change the reality. The Strait of Hormuz remains blocked and will ⁠not be reopened until Iran’s conditions are accepted." Those include removing economic sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

Ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Monday. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)

The U.S. lifted its blockade of Iran's shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran's primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on ‌its energy infrastructure.

Washington previously said it would lift the Iranian blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.

Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and "hit Iran hard," although he has thus far resisted deploying ground troops or seizing strategic islands and bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested ​he would rely on economic means, rather than military action.

On Thursday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the United States will soon announce measures that ​have "never been seen" on Iran.

"Watch this space ​for more announcements coming ⁠next ⁠week because ‌we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the ⁠history of economic isolation on a country," Bessent ‌said in an interview on on Newsmax's Rob Schmitt Tonight program.

"It will be a ​combination of economic isolation ⁠like the world has never ⁠seen before, and the continued ⁠blockade ⁠in ​the Strait of Hormuz that will ​keep ⁠anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports."

An unpopular war

Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices dragging down his approval ⁠ratings and potentially eroding his party's control of Congress in midterm elections in November.

WATCH | Trump responds to reports of U.S. military running low on munitions: Trump says U.S. brimming with weapons, vows to 'hunt down' leakers | Duration 2:08 U.S. President Donald dismissed reports of America's military running low on munitions due to the war with Iran, and said whoever leaked the information to U.S. media outlets will be 'hunted down' and given 'long term jail sentences.'

The U.S. has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and ⁠entities that it says are helping it procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.

Stress ⁠is ⁠mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on ​Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or around four per cent, this year.

Just a month ago, the agency ​had forecast a drop of 3.7 million barrels ⁠per day.

Oil prices settled down more than two per cent on Thursday after a week of gain, as investers focused on signs of weaker global demand and a sharp increase in U.S. crude inventories.

But reports that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones unsettled the market, renewing concerns about a widening regional war.

Global economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth as a result of the war, and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, ⁠warning that the impact will grow if the ‌war is not ended soon.

World.title: Carney, Trump to be given 'options' following latest trade talks, says U.S. rep
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said both U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney will now be given "options" following trade talks between Canadian and U.S. trade officials on Thursday.

"The president, the prime minister, obviously they'll be given options and discussions," Greer said, in what is the clearest indication yet about how the negotiations are going from the Trump administration's perspective.

Greer, who spoke to CBC News exclusively following the talks, called the meetings "good" and "cordial."

"We are going to speak with the president. I believe Canadian officials will speak with the prime minister," Greer added in French.

Following the meeting, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters he would "continue to do the work Canadians expect us to do."

LeBlanc didn't give a timeline as to how many more meetings there would be with Greer, adding "we'll have as many meetings as it takes."

CBC News has also learned that LeBlanc will brief the federal government's Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations on Friday afternoon to update them on how the negotiations are going, according to two sources with knowledge of tomorrow's meeting.

The committee serves as a forum where members can develop strategy for how Canada should approach its economic relationship with the U.S.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, right, and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette take part in a news conference during the G7 summit in June. The two met again on Thursday with U.S. trade officials. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

LeBlanc will also brief provinces on Friday, according to Louise Blais, Quebec's envoy for the review of the CUSMA, who shared the details during an interview with Radio-Canada.

Both LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette met with Greer this afternoon. It was the second meeting this week between the Canadian and American trade officials, and the fourth in just three weeks.

The two sides have ramped up discussions since Trump threatened to impose 50 per cent duties on hundreds of Canadian goods, on top of sectoral tariffs already in place. Those tariffs are slated to come into effect Aug. 19.

Following this afternoon's meeting, Charette returned to the U.S. Trade Representative office to continue discussions with her counterpart late into the evening, a source told CBC News.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

As previously reported, sources on both sides of the border say the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see.

The Americans are also seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and which covers security and energy, the sources said.

CBC News previously reported LeBlanc and Greer are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

However, sources also told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Those tariffs, according to the U.S. government, are due to a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

The Canadian side is willing to offer movement on some of those concerns, according to industry sources with knowledge of the situation. In addition to ending the booze bans, Canada is also considering lifting retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and making some changes on dairy.

Ford open to putting U.S. booze back on shelves

Also Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford — a frequent critic of Trump — said he'd be "more than happy" to bring U.S. booze back onto his province's shelves if a fair deal is reached that protects Ontario's steel, auto, forestry, agriculture and manufacturing sectors.

Ford also said his message to Americans is "a tariff on Canada is a tax on the American people."

"Remember when it comes to the [U.S.] midterms, you have to get that bully and send him a message," Ford said.

The Ontario premier's comments on U.S. alcohol bans echo those from Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette's office, who said in a statement last week the removal of U.S. alcohol from Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ) outlets will remain in effect "until an agreement that we deem fair has been negotiated."

"The sale of alcohol falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Quebec government. Quebec, and Quebec alone, will make that decision," the statement says.

World.title: Investors sue Selena Gomez for alleged fraud over mental health startup
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Singer and actor Selena Gomez was sued on Thursday by investors who say she committed fraud by failing to fulfil duties to build and promote her mental health startup.

The plaintiffs invested nearly $1.2 ​million US ($ 1.67 million) in Wondermind Global, which was ​launched in 2021 with a pitch to help users strengthen their "mental fitness," according to the lawsuit filed ​in federal court in Delaware.

Investors said they ⁠were told Gomez, ⁠one of the ‌biggest celebrities on social media with more than 500 million followers, would be actively involved in building the company as head of marketing. ⁠They argue Gomez and other company leaders failed to deliver on promises, including creating a mobile app.

"Gomez ‌purported to sign a contract obligating her to perform and then ignored it," the lawsuit says.

"There was no legitimate enterprise in the ​works, much less a lucrative one," the plaintiffs add, saying the company failed to meet "even its most basic ⁠obligations, such as timely paying its employees and ⁠vendors."

A ⁠representative for Gomez ​did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ​lawsuit argues that ⁠the plaintiffs were unaware of the company's troubles until an online news story detailed them in September 2025. Plaintiffs are seeking to recoup their investments and legal ⁠fees.
