World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU annual report: “serious problems” in Azerbaijan and “serious restrictions” on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Farmers rejoice as 'once-in-a-lifetime' wet season follows drought
World.content:
After successive years of devastating drought, South Australia's grain farmers say they are now experiencing some of the best conditions for growing crops in their lifetime.

Some farms have already received more than double their total rainfall for 2024 and 2025, while further rain at the start of August has pushed optimism for a bumper harvest to new heights.

While there are still several weeks left of the growing season and frost remains a risk, farmers say the potential for a big SA grain crop is "massive" after the past two dry years pushed many growers to the wall.

On parts of the state's Eyre Peninsula, some farmers have almost tripled last year's rainfall.

Mr Williams says recent rain has "set us up for spring" – a most crucial time for crops. (ABC Rural: Brooke Neindorf)

Streaky Bay farmer Dion Williams said the more than 400mm of rain he has received so far this year was a "staggering" amount for the district.

"I've been doing this for 28 years and I honestly feel like this could be a once-in-a-lifetime year … personally, as a family farm," Mr Williams said.

"Everyone's taking photos of their crops and sharing them, and I'm all for it, it's great. You've got to celebrate the good times."

Massive turnaround

He said 2026 was "chalk and cheese" compared to last year.

"When you get 120mm on the end of February, and everything starts to grow, your optimism starts to grow, especially after the last two years," Mr Williams said.

"We did get a get out of jail free card last year with some reasonable crops on the rainfall we had, but the year before was an absolute disaster."

Wheat crops are looking fantastic on SA's Eyre Peninsula after some very welcome rain. (Supplied: Dion Williams)

More than 400mm of rain has fallen in 2026 on Chris Lymn's farm at Wudinna, where he grows lentils and barley.

"Never before — haven't seen before in my time, so it's a fantastic year," Mr Lymn said.

"Early break, perfect conditions, crops in and up as early as you'd like to go — couldn't have asked for any better, really.

"We're all ready to make hay while the sun shines.

"We're a bit dubious as farmers to say we don't want more rain, but certainly we're a long way towards it. Normally we'd be looking for a September rain to finish; this rain this weekend means that we can probably just make do with a cool finish and we'll be pretty happy.

"We'd never say no, but I'd say we're pretty well home and hosed."

Confidence booming

Cungena farmer Miles Tomney received an early break of 138mm in late February — almost his total rainfall for 2024 in one event — and has since ticked over 450mm to date.

"It might be one out of the box we might not ever see again," Mr Tomney said.

"Confidence is up. Everyone's got a positive outlook at the moment, hopefully for everything the frosts stay away and everyone gets a piece of it [the rain].

"Everywhere I've driven across the state, no-one's missing out, so it's South Australia's turn by the looks."

Tim Paschke's paddocks were bare dirt and sand this time last year. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

One district that has experienced a remarkable turnaround is SA's Riverland, where farmers this time last year were staring at bare, dusty paddocks.

Waikerie grower Tim Paschke is this year relieved to see healthy canola and lentil crops swaying in the breeze.

He described the more than 30mm of rain that fell on his farm in the past week as "a real blessing" at a critical time.

"[It's] one of the best August rains we can remember for such a long time, compared to last year when we didn't even have our paddocks covered," Mr Pashke said.

Mr Pashke grows canola, lentils, barley and wheat in the SA's Riverland. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

"It's been an absolute game changer. When you get such a soaking rain, it does so much for the soil, and it's just such a load off our minds; we're very happy.

" There's some real positives for us, and obviously my bank balance really needs a bit of a kick because it's been three pretty tough years up here. "

The exact same paddocks that were bare in August 2025 are now lush, exactly a year later. (Supplied: Tim Paschke)

Agronomist Jake Hull believed some wheat crops could more than double the average yield this year — but cautioned that the season wasn't over yet.

"It is a sight to behold. The potential is massive," Mr Hull said.

"I like to keep reality in check, and we've still got a little way to go … but this last lot of rain has definitely raised that level of optimism to another level."

World.title: Albanese says Trump giving 'consideration' to tariff exemption after phone call
World.content:
The prime minister has used a rare phone call with Donald Trump to press for an exemption from the administration's latest round of sweeping tariffs, saying the US president has agreed to give "consideration" to his request.

Anthony Albanese called a snap press conference this morning after an overnight phone call with Mr Trump, the first since their extraordinary late-night exchange in March over the fate of Iranian female footballers in Australia.

The ABC was told the call went for about 40 minutes, and Mr Albanese described the conversation as "productive, constructive … and substantial".

The federal government complained loudly in July when the Trump administration announced a 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from Australia as part of a global regime of import taxes on countries the US claims have failed to remove forced labour from supply chains.

New 12.5pc US tariff for Australia A new levy on exports from Australia into the US has taken effect, superseding the 10 per cent tariff that was expiring. Dozens of other countries have also been hit, but Australia's tariff is among the highest.

Australia maintains there is "no credible evidentiary basis" for the move, and senior government ministers believe the administration is simply trying to find a workaround after the Supreme Court struck down its 10 per cent tariffs in February.

Mr Albanese said he urged Mr Trump to "consider a full exemption" for Australia, or "at the very least no increase" from the old 10 per cent tariff rate.

"I informed him about our record when it comes to dealing with issues such as modern slavery, the strengthening that we have put forward as well, to look and hold companies accountable for the supply chain process as well," Mr Albanese said.

He said he did not put his request in "ideological" terms, but stressed the scale of Australian investment in the United States and that "over 20 years the US has had a trade surplus with Australia of US$442 billion".

"I put the argument very much to the president, as a friend of the United States, we would request that to be considered," he said.

" We have a different position when it comes to tariffs and, of course, our position as a government is that tariffs are an economic imposition and a cost on the countries that are imposing them. "

He did not sound optimistic about Mr Trump budging, saying the two sides have "a different view" on tariffs, but said the US president promised to give "consideration" to his request.

Leaders discuss Iran war and AUKUS

Anthony Albanese speaks to the media about his phone call with Donald Trump. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The two men also discussed the war in Iran, with Mr Albanese telling journalists that he reiterated Australia's call for the conflict to be brought to an end.

Analysts say the US is now stuck in a quagmire in Iran with no clear exit strategy, while talks over Tehran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz remain bogged down.

Mr Albanese said Mr Trump gave him an "extensive update" on the progress of the war, and "expressed his confidence going forward".

The two men also discussed AUKUS, with Mr Albanese saying they agreed the nuclear submarine program remained "full steam ahead".

And Mr Albanese told journalists that he raised China's recent ballistic missile test in the Pacific, which has stirred unease among several nations across the Pacific and has been sharply criticised by several Western nations and US allies.

He said Mr Trump responded by observing that the missile test "caused a great deal of concern right across the Pacific, which is true".

The prime minister said he also briefed the US president about the host of new treaties which Australia had struck across the Pacific recently.

World.title: Live: Australia hunting quick wickets against brave Bangladesh
World.content:
Good morning Henry and Simon! I’m hoping Australia can get their act together today as yesterday definitely wasn’t our best ever performance 😬 I’ll be at day 1 of the Mackay test so I’m hoping to see some better cricket by then…. - Tanya

G'day Tanya!

It was pretty dire stuff from Australia yesterday.

I think the lack of care with the bat was the most disappointing aspect from an Australian perspective, especially in comparison with how composed and considered Bangladesh seemed in reaching 1-96 at stumps.

Sure, the ball was nipping around a bit early on and the Bangladeshi seamers were sensational, but I don't think that was a sub-200 first-dig pitch.

And then, it was concerning how quickly the Australian bowlers seemed to run out of both steam and ideas.

It was undoubtedly muggy out there, but during the final hour of play, there was very little zip in the field and the bowlers didn't really seem convinced they were likely to take a wicket.

We're moments away from the start of play on day two.

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly when the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was red-carded for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after La Liga hosts Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, Fulham walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on believing there should be a penalty shootout to decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a drawn match.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

World.title: Victorian Coalition says it would not accelerate end of coal power
World.content:
The Victorian Coalition says it will not accelerate the closure of the state's coal-fired power stations if it wins at the state election later this year.

National Party member for Morwell Martin Cameron announced the plan yesterday, with the Nationals citing Victorian Auditor-General warnings that the state could face electricity shortfalls when the Yallourn Power Station closes in 2028.

Mr Cameron told the ABC the Labor government's ambition to close Loy Yang A power plant in 2035 with renewable wind and solar was not tracking well, but conceded there were no discussions to bring forward the closure of any plants.

He said the Coalition's announcement was not to build new coal plants, but to keep the existing power stations firing as long as possible.

"To keep the lights on for everybody, we're going to still have to rely on our coal-fired generators in the Latrobe Valley to supply a consistent, constant base load power for Victoria," he said.

"It's not asking for more coal plants.

"It's letting the current coal plants that we do have in Loy Yang A and B running to their end of life or until there is enough power in the system from other forms of energy to take over the system, and guarantee Victorians that we have enough power to run manufacturing businesses and the family home because we want to keep the lights on at the end of the day."

A number of coal-fired energy plants are based in Gippsland's Latrobe Valley, and are slated for closure in the coming years, with EnergyAustralia's Yallourn plant to close in 2028.

Martin Cameron has reaffirmed the Coalition's commitment to keeping coal-fired power stations going until their retirement date. (ABC News)

Retirement plans on track

The ABC confirmed with Loy Yang operator Alinta Energy there were no changes to the plan to retire the power station in 2035.

There was also no firm date for the closure of the Loy Yang B plant, while the Hazelwood site closed in March 2017.

A spokesperson for Yallourn power station operator EnergyAustralia said the plant was still set to retire at the end of June 2028.

"We gave seven years' notice so the market, AEMO and governments had time to prepare, and we're invested to keep the plant running reliably right through to retirement," the spokesperson said.

"EnergyAustralia is developing plans for the Yallourn Energy Security Precinct, an early-stage proposal looking at gas generation, large-scale battery storage and data centre development, using the site's existing grid connections, gas infrastructure and skilled workforce.

"Alongside that, our 350MW Wooreen battery is currently under construction, with operations expected in 2027, ahead of the closure."

A Victorian government spokesperson said renewable energy remained the "most cost-effective way" to replace coal plants.

"Our plan is delivering cheaper renewable energy for Victorians — keeping power bills down and the lights on," the spokesperson said.

"We've provided long-term certainty around coal closure dates to ensure that the system is ready — AEMO and VicGrid have been preparing for Yallourn's closure since it was announced in 2021."

Drop in coal power last year

State government data showed Victoria exceeded its 2025 renewable energy target, with renewables delivering 44 per cent of the state's electricity generation that year.

According to the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO), Victorian brown coal-fired generation dropped to all-time lows in the last quarter of the year, driven by lower availability.

Director of the Victoria Energy Policy Centre at Victoria University Professor Bruce Mountain said there was no prospect coal-powered plants slated for closure in 2028 would be shut down sooner than expected.

"If anything, the opposite is the case, the Victorian government having contracted with EnergyAustralia to possibly extend the operation of the plant after 2028," Professor Mountain said.

Bruce Mountain says it is possible that coal plants could remain open longer. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

"I think the planned closure of 1000mW at the Yallourn plant in 2028 looks increasingly likely that the market can accommodate that, in a similar way to the way it accommodated the Hazelwood closure in 2017.

"I do think the subsequent closure of either of the Loy Yang plants in the next five years is extremely problematic. Victoria then will definitely have capacity shortfalls."

Environment Victoria climate campaign manager Joy Toose said the Coalition's pledge was doubling down on "the aging, unreliable infrastructure that's causing the problem in the first place".

"Last summer a quarter of Victoria's coal capacity was offline at any given time, spiking out electricity prices," she said.

"Renewable energy is already the cheapest power in the system, roughly half the wholesale cost of coal and gas. If the Nationals were serious about protecting Victorians from blackouts and high bills, they'd be backing projects that get that cheap power to households, not attacking them."

World.title: Air safety boss 'trying to understand' Sydney Airport incident reporting delay
World.content:
The nation's air safety boss has questioned why it took four days for another safety incident at Sydney Airport to be reported to investigators.

Air Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) chief commissioner Angus Mitchell told the ABC he was only notified of Sunday's incident about lunchtime on Thursday.

The most recent incident last Sunday involved two planes more than kilometre away crossing the same runway ahead of take-off.

Air Services Australia said the two aircraft were never in close proximity and was working with the ATSB to investigate the incident.

"The two aircraft didn't come within really probably around a thousand metres of each other. But, notwithstanding that, it shouldn't have occurred," Mr Mitchell told on 702 ABC Sydney.

Chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said ATSB would look at the circumstances leading to the incidents. (Supplied: ATSB)

"We're still trying to understand exactly what the delay in the reporting to us was."

He said the delay may have been caused over confusion about whether the incident was a training exercise.

"But it's not unusual to have trainees in all types of aviation to, at some stage, get exposure to live environments under supervision," he said.

'Rarely a single point of failure'

Mr Mitchell said there were "multiple lines of defence" in an emergency situation like the three recent incidents.

"I will say in all three instances, there was a layer of defence that kicked in and prevented an escalation," he said.

"We find in a lot of our investigations it is very rarely a single point of failure. For it to progress through to an actual accident, multiple things need to go wrong.

"Equally in this one, this latest one that was reported to us, a traffic control cancelled the take-off clearance around the same time as the pilot on board realise there was a potential conflict."

It comes after two near-misses at Sydney Airport in the space of a fortnight.

The first on July 27 saw a Qantas Link and Qantas flight avoid a collision.

The Jetstar flight had to brake on the tarmac of Sydney Airport to avoid colliding with a Qatar Airlines flight on Sunday. (Supplied)

The second, also last Sunday about three hours before the latest incident to come to light, saw a Jetstar crew member injured after pilots were forced to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding into a Qatar Airlines flight.

Two ground crew involved were stood down and underwent blood and alcohol testing as part of the ATSB investigation.

The incidents saw renewed calls for change from the Civil Air, whose president Scott Nugent said there were air traffic controllers in Australia and it was putting pressure on services.

The near-misses resulted in Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp summoned to Canberra to meet with Transport Minister Catherine King.

World.title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
World.content:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP

World.title: Kangaroo drownings in canal spark community concern
World.content:
Driving down a country road near the Riverina town of Nericon, the first thing that hits is the putrid smell.

WARNING: This story contains images of dead animals that may be distressing for readers.

Eight kangaroo carcasses are visible, five in the water and three on the bank side of the canal where they have all drowned.

"In winter it's actually gotten worse, I'm seeing more and more carcasses," said resident and bus driver Anita Tovo.

Anita Tovo says it is upsetting to see so many kangaroos dying when solutions exist. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

The high-density polyethylene (HDPE) sheets that line the banks of the Murrumbidgee Irrigation-owned canal were first installed in 2019 to prevent water loss.

Fencing was installed at the same time.

The plastic-lined canal and fencing trap the kangaroos, leaving them little opportunity to escape. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

"I never saw kangaroos in here … before the plastic lining and fencing [was installed]. I think it's about five years now that I've really taken notice," Ms Tovo said.

The only open area for kangaroos to exit the canal is a few kilometres further on where the fencing stops and rocks line the bank.

In a statement, Murrumbidgee Irrigation (MI) said fencing, cameras and escape structures known as egress points were in place at regular intervals along the canal and were being monitored.

"While these channels are essential for ensuring efficient and sustainable water use, we do acknowledge that they can unintentionally impact local wildlife," it said.

The only open area where kangaroos can escape is kilometres downstream, but many do not make it that far. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

While some cameras are visible at the canal, Ms Tovo said she was still finding dead kangaroos regularly.

"How many are dying, how many are being saved, how many are noticed going in and how quick are you [Murrumbidgee Irrigation] to come out to save them?" she said.

Ms Tovo said she had seen the occasional loosely placed rubber mat or rope ladder, but she said neither provided adequate assistance to the kangaroos.

The kangaroos that drown upstream end up floating down to the regulator. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

'Near impossible' for wildlife rescuers

WIRES spokesperson John Grant said when they started getting repeat reports about kangaroos in this canal, they knew something was not right.

"We don't tend to get a lot of calls about kangaroos in canals, certainly not like the amount that we've had with this," he said.

Mr Grant said resources are stretched in rural NSW and saving a drowning kangaroo was near impossible.

"Because our closest volunteer is at least an hour away from Nericon, when she arrived, twice I think it was that she went there, they had already drowned," he said.

Three kangaroos were pulled from the canal on New Farms Road after drowning. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Kangaroos are a protected species in every Australian state, and while it is not uncommon to see them on the roadside after being hit by a car, Mr Grant said this was different.

"This isn't a random accident," he said.

"This is an ongoing issue where these kangaroos continue to drown presumably because there isn't enough infrastructure for them to be able to get out of a canal that's been lined with black plastic."

There are currently no state regulations relating to egress points and animal welfare in canals.

Solutions available

Kylie Soanes says animal drownings in canals are a nationwide problem, with plastic lining exacerbating the issue. (ABC News: Rhiannon Stevens)

A research fellow in urban biodiversity at the University of Melbourne, Kylie Soanes, said waterway designs should keep native wildlife in mind.

"The ground is flat and then all of a sudden there's just a steep drop into this irrigation canal, and there's none of that sloping edge that would allow animals to escape that we might see in any kind of natural waterway," she said.

" It's very fair to say that the plastic exacerbates the danger of these canals. "

Dr Soanes said countries like the Netherlands, which is famous for its canals, were an example of what can be done to prevent these types of animal deaths.

"They [the Netherlands] cut escape ramps into the edge of the canal and line them with rocks and create a bit more of a slope," she said.

"So if an animal is drifting along a deep section of canal, they'll be able to find their feet and get out."

Dr Soanes said fencing was also an important solution to the problem, and while there was no one-size-fits-all fence for every animal, they should cater to the local wildlife.

"Because there's so much land on one side of the fence, they can get a good run up, which allows them to propel themselves over the fence and into the canal area. But once they're in, there's not a lot of wiggle room," she said.

"So it either needs to be high enough to completely exclude kangaroos … or there need to be escape ramps that allow any animals that have accidentally found themselves in the channel corridor to get themselves out."

Drowned kangaroos are a too-common sight in the Nericon canal. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Ms Tovo said something needed to change.

She said she and members of WIRES had met with Murray Irrigation to discuss the issues, but nothing further had come from the meeting.

"There's got to be consultation with [animal] welfare organisations because I'm sitting here and I can smell those carcasses and we can see what's happening because people don't care."

MI said it was committed to ongoing improvement and was continuing to assess infrastructure to identify further ways to enhance animal safety.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘C’ gives evidence as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day eight of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Peter Rae

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing and progressing to touching. On the Crown’s case, “J” was aged between 17 and 21 at the time of the nine alleged indecent assaults.

The defence case is that the alleged incidents didn’t happen.

This week, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they said he told them about the alleged assaults, and his mother and his former coach gave evidence yesterday.

His mother testified that “J” initially told her that Jones had not touched him, before telling her the following year that he had lied. She said that she was in shock when “J” made the disclosure, and she told her son she should have protected him.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Australia v Bangladesh LIVE: Smith admits he was out, as Starc and Cummins chase early wickets
World.content:
Steve Smith admitted he was given a second life by technology after playing a lone hand in Australia’s frail innings on day one of the first Test in Darwin, before Bangladesh took on their bowlers with class.

World.title: Westpac director says bank’s board was kept in dark over KPMG allegations
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesConsulting Westpac director says bank’s board was kept in dark over KPMG allegations Colin Kruger August 14, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Lendlease chair and current Westpac board member Michael Ullmer has told a parliamentary committee how the only warning of the KPMG whistleblower allegations relating to the bank was made to fellow director Peter Nash, who did not tell the rest of the bank’s board. The board did not hear of the allegations until Labor Senator Deborah O’Neill read them out in parliament in March this year. Nash, a former KPMG partner, resigned due to perceived conflicts last month. He stayed at the home of KPMG chairman Martin Sheppard as the firm was preparing its pitch for the $25 million-a-year audit contract. KPMG had told Nash there was no issue to be concerned about. Westpac director Michael Ullmer speaks at the inquiry. Alex Ellinghausen “He resigned because of the fact of those social contacts that we became aware of, when at the beginning of the process we made it very clear to members of the subcommittee and to people involved that there should be no form of social contact during the tender process,” Ullmer told the committee. “I believe he did fail because that was clearly something that should not have occurred during the process.”



Related Article Analysis

Consulting The humiliation of KPMG’s lawyers is almost complete Ullmer told O’Neill that is was not until May 13 that “our general counsel at Westpac got the first comprehensive explanation of what the allegations were at that time. But it was conveyed again as something that had been fully investigated, and they were not substantiated.” Former RBA governor and Macquarie chairman Glenn Stevens is also being called before the hearing. Optus chairman John Arthur and chief executive Stephen Rue are also due to appear at the probe into the spiralling scandal that has purged the most senior ranks at KPMG over the misuse of confidential clients’ information for commercial gain. Ullmer revealed the frustration over the drip feed of information which slowly revealed just how serious the matter was. “That has been one of the most challenging aspects of this matter because you think you have your arms around it, and then more information is revealed,” Ullmer said.



Ullmer was chairman of Lendlease when senior KPMG executives accessed sensitive board documents about the tender of its lucrative audit business. KPMG was later awarded the audit work for Westpac. He ridiculed a statement O’Neill read out from internal KPMG communications on the matter stating that there was no such thing as “Chinese walls”, the so-called ethical walls meant to protect sensitive client information from wrongful exploitation. “I think that’s a ridiculous statement to make because there obviously have to be Chinese walls or ethical walls,” he said. Former RBA chief and current Macquarie chair Glenn Stevens is among those due to appear. Peter Braig “You expect that the confidential information, the secrets that they gain access to, will remain confidential.”



Dexus chairman Warwick Negus also appeared before the committee and refuted KPMG claims that it was allowed to use sensitive information it possessed from conducting the company’s internal audit work to pitch for its external audit. “I think when we denied Miss (Eileen) Hoggett participation in the internal audit meeting, where she wanted to learn more about Dexus to inform their bid, when we said that was inappropriate, I think that that was a pretty obvious signal,” Negus said. Hoggett, KPMG’s former chief operating officer, was expelled last month after the firm said new evidence had been identified to support the whistleblower’s allegation that sensitive Lendlease board documents were kept in a locker in KPMG’s Sydney office. Law firm Allens did not talk to Dexus about any of the allegations when it conducted an investigation and Negus did not see the law firm’s report until it was published this week. Stevens is expected to be grilled over how the firm won its $70 million a year audit contract, the biggest in Australia.



Related Article Consulting Former RBA governor dragged into KPMG scandal Last month, Stevens dropped a bombshell on the KPMG scandal, telling shareholders the group is reviewing the embattled firm’s capability to deliver on the lucrative Macquarie audit tender it won last year, due to the exodus of senior staff over the scandal. Macquarie has also instigated an external review of KPMG’s pursuit of the contract, which was valued at $69 million last year. World.title: The story behind Hawks star’s goggles; Demon leads side to glory in first match in 355 days
World.content:
One of the more striking sights from Thursday night’s AFLW clash was Hawks gun Jas Fleming crashing through packs wearing what looked like clear goggles.

This was not a fashion statement but a protective measure, after Fleming copped an accidental footy to the eye during pre-season which meant she barely played during the leadup to round 1.

Jas Fleming in her protective glasses. AFL Photos via Getty Images

It’s not the first time we’ve seen a player wear protective glasses, of course. It’s regulation attire for Fremantle big man and former Pie Mason Cox, who was told to wear them or risk blindness if he copped another eye injury.

Fleming, the daughter of former Australian cricketer Damien, wasn’t hindered by the goggles. She had 14 disposals but what stood out was her toughness in the contest and penetrative kicking. It wasn’t enough to stop the Hawks being overrun by Melbourne, who won by 19 points.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Dallas McInerney continues giving evidence after denying Angus Taylor wanted to fund NSW Reformers
World.content:
Dallas McInerney has told the commission repeatedly that he did his due diligence when securing a contract with Reformers-linked company Beckington, which he says was for genuine work.

Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin has just shown McInerney evidence that when McInerney asked Christian Ellis to provide an ABN for his company, Ellis instead provided one registered to his sister, Dr Samantha Ellis.

McInerney said he believed at the time that the ABN belonged to Beckington but relied on his finance department to check it.

“Can I suggest to you that the due diligence that was conducted between April and August wasn’t particularly effective?” Curtin said.

“It would appear that there was a missing step there. I accept that,” McInerney said.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘C’ gives evidence as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day eight of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Peter Rae

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing and progressing to touching. On the Crown’s case, “J” was aged between 17 and 21 at the time of the nine alleged indecent assaults.

The defence case is that the alleged incidents didn’t happen.

This week, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they said he told them about the alleged assaults, and his mother and his former coach gave evidence yesterday.

His mother testified that “J” initially told her that Jones had not touched him, before telling her the following year that he had lied. She said that she was in shock when “J” made the disclosure, and she told her son she should have protected him.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
