World.title: The story behind Hawks star’s goggles; Demon leads side to glory in first match in 355 days
World.content:
One of the more striking sights from Thursday night’s AFLW clash was Hawks gun Jas Fleming crashing through packs wearing what looked like clear goggles.

This was not a fashion statement but a protective measure, after Fleming copped an accidental footy to the eye during pre-season which meant she barely played during the leadup to round 1.

Jas Fleming in her protective glasses. AFL Photos via Getty Images

It’s not the first time we’ve seen a player wear protective glasses, of course. It’s regulation attire for Fremantle big man and former Pie Mason Cox, who was told to wear them or risk blindness if he copped another eye injury.

Fleming, the daughter of former Australian cricketer Damien, wasn’t hindered by the goggles. She had 14 disposals but what stood out was her toughness in the contest and penetrative kicking. It wasn’t enough to stop the Hawks being overrun by Melbourne, who won by 19 points.

World.title: 'Relentlessly optimistic': Luxon looks past coup attempt as election campaign resumes
World.content:
The Prime Minister hasn't referenced his tumultuous week at all in a speech at the Business Canterbury election conference, focusing instead on the state of the world and National's plans in the South Island.

"Two and a half years into this job, I remain relentlessly optimistic about New Zealand," Christopher Luxon says.

Luxon survived a confidence vote on Wednesday - the second in four months - and remained the leader of the National Party, and prime minister, following a leadership challenge.

As though the confidence vote never happened, Luxon spoke of economic management and the "two broad reinforcing actions that we desperately need".

"The first is ensuring that we have financial discipline and resilience, and the second is improving economic productivity."

He also referenced the Budget Responsibility Rules the party announced last weekend, including net core crown debt below 40 percent, which a leading economist called the least ambitious it could possibly be.

Luxon also took aim at what he called Labour's economic agenda of "spend more, tax more, borrow more", saying that doesn't work out as people claim.

"It ends in higher debt. It ends in higher taxes. It ends in higher interest rates, and a country, frankly, less able to protect its own people when the inevitable shock comes along."

He also used the speech to announce National's "plan for the South Island".

Luxon said it was "easy for a politician to tell you what they're going to do", but a "different thing to ask you to judge them on their track record".

"But that's actually what I want you to do because National is the party of delivery."

Policy announcement

The National Party wants to bolster growth in the South Island if re-elected, making a range of commitments in infrastructure, energy and public services.

The party would develop a new Government Policy Statement (GPS) on mining and extraction, create a requirement for data centre projects to also include new, firmed generation and deliver 96 additional beds for patients at Christchurch Hospital.

The package would also make public transport funding available for congestion reducing Gondola solutions in Queenstown.

Luxon made the announcement during his speech at the Business Canterbury election conference on Friday.

He called the South Island a "powerhouse" of the New Zealand economy.

RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"There's a lot going well in the south, but there's more we can do to unlock its full potential."

The GPS on mining would be modelled off similar ones created for grocery competition, and make clear that "mining and extractive activities have regional and national benefits qualifying them to access the Fast-track regime".

The requirement for new data centres would mean "the development of digital infrastructure doesn't put upward pressure on power prices for households and businesses, while giving energy developers the committed customers they need to finance new generation".

RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

The party would finish fitting out Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital, adding the extra beds, at an estimated cost of $70 million.

The building was currently being constructed, "the rooms are there, but not finished off", the party said.

"National will complete them now, so all 96 beds are ready for patients straight away instead of waiting - adding real capacity to the South Island's largest hospital as Canterbury grows."

'Delay after delay' - Labour

The Labour party says National has spent nearly three years neglecting the South Island, with campaign chair Kieran McAnulty saying everything it announced today "should already be underway."

"Instead, South Islanders have had delay after delay, downgrade after downgrade, and a Government that has treated the South Island as an afterthought," said McAnulty.

"After ignoring the South Island for most of this term, it's like they suddenly remembered it exists and dipped behind the back of the sofa to see what promises they could dust off.

World.title: Sylvia Park shooting: Man fatally shot by police was on community detention
World.content:
A man who was fatally shot by police as he approached Auckland's Sylvia Park Shopping Centre while carrying a stolen air rifle was on community detention and supervision, RNZ can reveal.

RNZ has seen a number of tribute posts online for the man who died.

RNZ understands the 33-year-old had four previous convictions for firearms offences and was sentenced to four years in prison in 2023 for aggravated robbery.

After being released in 2025, he stole more than $1000 worth of goods from Rebel Sports and was serving a sentence of four months community detention and supervision.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

It is understood he was on this sentence when he was shot dead on Thursday.

He was facing a charge of taking a Subaru Legacy when he was killed and appeared in court less than a month ago.

In response to questions from RNZ, Corrections director of communities, partnerships and pathways Simon Chaplin said Corrections' thoughts were with those impacted by the incident at Sylvia Park.

"Corrections can confirm this person was subject to community detention and supervision.

A screen has been put up outside Footlocker on Friday. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"Their community sentence included a 7pm-7am curfew where electronic monitoring was used to verify that they were at their home address during the hours of this curfew. They were not in breach of this curfew at the time the Sylvia Park incident occurred."

Corrections was reviewing its involvement with the man.

"It would not be appropriate for us to provide further information while this and the police reviews are ongoing."

According to Corrections' website community detention is a "punitive sentence that restricts an offender's movements during their curfew". The offenders are subject to electronic monitoring and/or GPS, and they must wear an anklet at all times during their sentence.

Some of Footlocker's window panes have been covered. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"It requires an offender to remain at an approved residence at certain times specified by the court. This is known as the offender's curfew.

"Electronic monitoring equipment is installed at the offender's address and their compliance with their curfew is electronically monitored for the duration of the sentence."

Offenders can be sentenced to community detention for between 14 days and six months.

Gun City owner David Tipple, where police say the man stole the air rifle from, told RNZ staff chased the man after the theft.

Tipple said the man was being shown the empty air rifle when he grabbed it and ran, with the staff going after him.

"One staff member got close to catching him but the man succeeded in driving off in a car."

Tipple said no one has ever done this in their 48 years of business.

He raised concerns about public blame.

"People seek to blame an inanimate object which is responsibly used by hundreds of thousands of law abiding New Zealanders instead of looking into why this man, known to the courts, was able to place the public, and himself, in danger," Tipple said.

Superintendent Sunny Patel earlier said police had received information about the theft of an air rifle from Gun City in Penrose around 2pm on Thursday.

Police vehicles and the Eagle helicopter were dispatched to the area, locating the car near Sylvia Park.

Spikes were successfully deployed but the car continued towards Mount Wellington Highway, still being driven in an erratic manner, Patel said.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Police confronted the man underneath an overpass as he approached the entrance of Sylvia Park, still carrying the air rifle. He was then shot by police.

Patel confirmed police were carrying out a critical incident investigation. He also confirmed the IPCA had been notified and would be carrying out its own investigation.

He said it was not known whether the air rifle was loaded, or whether the man had any ammunition.

Patel was not aware of how many times the man was shot, whether there had been any attempt to detain him or whether he had aimed the weapon at anyone.

"That's something that will need to be uncovered when we carry out the full investigation, when we've actually spoken to the police officers involved," he said on Thursday night.

The decision to shoot rested with the officer at the scene, and no clearance was required, he said.

"Our investigation is still at the very early stages of piecing together the events," he said.

Superintendent Sunny Patel (file image). RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Patel could not comment on whether the man had threatened staff at the gun shop, or if staff had attempted to stop the man. The gun theft had been a shoplifting incident and the man had walked in through the front door.

The police investigation would look into what happened at the store, but it was concerning the man was able to steal a weapon, Patel said.

"We just don't know the circumstances of how he became in possession of that firearm.

"Until we've actually figured out the nature of the actual theft and how it occurred, it is of concern."

Police remain at the scene on Friday. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Patel said the man was alone, and they were not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

Witnesses or anyone with phone or dashcam footage were urged to come forward.

Patel said he was happy with police response times to the incident, and said they were providing support to the officer who fatally shot the man.

"We've put support in place for the officer concerned and that support will be ongoing. No one comes to work and expects this kind of result. Our staff work very, very hard on a daily basis to make sure the community is safe, and this is the last thing that they want to experience."

World.title: ACT Minister labels National's failed leadership coup a 'shit show'
World.content:
An ACT minister has labelled the National Party's failed leadership coup a "shit show".

ACT leader David Seymour read out the message he received from Andrew Hoggard during a media stand-up at the Business Canterbury election conference on Friday morning.

Seymour said "absolute legend Andrew Hoggard was way out" on the West Coast of the South Island, "out of range".

He then read out the message Hoggard sent.

"I actually want to read you the the message that he sent ... I'll just bring up the message," Seymour said.

"Been on the road for most of the day, visiting farmers. Haven't had any radio coverage and little reception. So just catching up on all this. Dot dot dot. What a shit show!"

Seymour said it was sent at 8.50pm on Wednesday night.

Biosecurity Minister and ACT MP Andrew Hoggard. RNZ / Kim Baker-Wilson

Seymour said it was too early to say whether National's leadership woes will impact support for the coalition.

"When it comes down to it, people want to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand's potential."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon didn't reference his tumultuous week at all during his speech at the conference, focusing instead on the state of the world and National's plans in the South Island.

World.title: Gisborne residents urged to be ready for flooding and slips
World.content:
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging residents to be ready for potential surface flooding, slips and more as heavy rain moves in.

An orange heavy rain warning is in effect for Gisborne/Tai Rāwhiti, north of Tolaga Bay, until 8pm on Friday night.

"That's in place this morning and 25 millimetres per hour rain rate can cause that rapid flooding. Some places are already seeing quite high rain rate," meteorologist Paris Mitchell said.

Between 90 and 120mm of rain is expected.

The public are being told to clear gutters and drains, steer clear of low-lying areas while the heaviest rain comes through, and drive to the conditions.

MetService said there is only a minimal chance of upgrading its warning to red.

The worst of the weather is forecast for the morning and afternoon - with a thunderstorm warning in place for then.

Gisborne mayor Rehette Stolz asked the public to report any flooding or slips amid heavy downpours.

She said it was very wet but Gisborne was prepared for anything, and civil defence teams were monitoring water levels and flooding.

She reminded people to be cautious and drive to conditions.

MetService said it has recorded up to 10mm of rain per hour already this morning in the northern ranges and 8mm around East Cape.

Earlier, MetService issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North.

World.title: Flights cancelled, delayed as fog restrictions hit Auckland Airport
World.content:
Fog restrictions are in place at Auckland Airport.

By 7.20am, several domestic regional flights had been cancelled as well as some arrivals.

A number departing had been delayed as well as arriving.

Of the main trunk domestic flights, one to Christchurch had been delayed, as had an arrival from Dunedin.

International flights have not been affected by the fog.

The airport said passengers are advised to check its website for the latest flight information.

Wellington seafog

MetService said seafog and low clouds in Wellington Harbour could disrupt flights.

A southerly wind is expected to push seafog towards the airport throughout the day.

Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said the southern coast of Wellington will be most exposed - including the harbour and airport.

"So you get that sea fog when sea surface temperatures and air temperatures are very close together.

"So with a southerly the air is cooled down, the sea takes a little bit longer to cool down water - it hangs on to heat better than air essentially."

He said low visibility might impact flights, depending on how much moisture builds in the air.

"Basically, planes like to see the ground before they land."

World.title: Demand for ethnic women’s refuge support nearly doubles in two years
World.content:
An ethnic women's refuge organisation says demand for its safe houses has nearly doubled over the past two years, with women facing increasingly complex barriers to getting help.

Shakti Women's Refuge has provided more than 7000 overnight spaces over the past two years, almost double the roughly 3600 spaces it provided in the preceding two-year period.

The organisation opened a third safe house in Auckland last month as it continues to see women and children seeking support, including women who face additional challenges because of their immigration status.

Founded in Auckland in 1995, Shakti has since grown into a national organisation, with branches in Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin.

"There's never a day when our safe houses are not full," said Shakti strategic development manager Shasha Ali.

Ali moved to New Zealand from Singapore with her family 25 years ago and has Singaporean, Indonesian and Punjabi heritage.

She said her own experience of family harm had also shaped her understanding of the issue.

The new safe house, she said, was a response to the growing number of women seeking help.

"Throughout the year there is always women and children requiring support," she said.

"Some of them are on a visa and they might have challenges to get support and social assistance otherwise and our safe houses are also designed to support women who are more vulnerable when it comes to their immigration status."

Ali said Shakti had also seen an increase in self-referrals over the past few years.

She said many of the cases the organisation had dealt with in the past involved culturally oppressive practices within South Asian communities, including dowry-related violence and honour-based violence.

However, the profile of women seeking help had changed.

"We are now seeing women who are highly educated also accessing our services," Ali said.

She said stigma around asking for help remained one of the biggest challenges in tackling family harm in South Asian communities.

Whether someone is a new migrant or has grown up in New Zealand, Ali said, the pressure around family honour and reputation could make it hard to seek help.

"At the end of the day, we're talking about family honour," she said.

"We're talking about the reputation of a family that might also be connected by caste or might be connected by the region that they've come from.

"These are the mindset challenges that women who need to break through and break away from the cycles of abuse have to sort of undergo before they come out."

Ali said that despite Shakti having operated for more than three decades, the organisation was still sometimes viewed as a "homewrecker".

She argued that communities needed to recognise that there was no home if a family was being held together through tolerance of abuse or inequality between women and men.

"We are proudly and unapologetically feminist in our approach when it comes to working with Asian African and Middle Eastern women and children," she said.

"And we stand by the fact that, at the end of the day, safety comes first."

Shasha Ali is strategic development manager at Shakti Women's Refuge. Supplied

Ali said Shakti supported women from their first call to escape violence, providing immediate safety support, legal and immigration assistance, financial support and advocacy until they are safe and ready to live independently in the community.

Another organisation working to support women and children experiencing family harm is Sahaayta Counselling Services.

Founded in 2013, Sahaayta began in Manurewa, providing counselling services to South Asian communities.

"Sahaayta was founded because we saw that there's an increasingly gap for counselling services especially among Indians, Pakistanis, Sri Lankans and other South Asian groups," said team leader of ethnic services Zoya Salim Kara.

Kara has worked as a counsellor for more than a decade.

Originally from Mumbai, she came to New Zealand from India in 2008 as an international student.

She said there was still a stigma around counselling among South Asian communities.

"We don't have the concept of counselling in the eastern cultures and we didn't have it while we were growing up," she said.

"You didn't have a counsellor or a psychologist. You directly saw a psychiatrist in India. So you literally had to have some underlying mental health or, you know, believed to be having severe mental health issues to see somebody or seek help.

"So, there's a lot of shame. There's a lot of stigma and it's still not normalised."

However, Sahaayta had found that when a service was able to build trust and provide ethical and confidential support, people were more likely to come forward.

Kara said she had also seen a rise in sexual harm among South Asian communities, particularly within the Indian community.

"Initially, years ago, we'd get a lot of physical abuse. We'd get verbal abuse, financial abuse. What we're seeing today increase every day is sexual harm," she said.

Women used to disclose sexual harm around their eighth or ninth counselling session, Kara said, but they were now more likely to talk about it during their second session.

She believed that could be because people were more aware that help was available and that they could talk about their experiences.

"If two clients disclose sexual violence to me eight years ago, now it's eight clients out of 10 that disclose sexual violence," Kara said.

Zoya Salim Kara has been a counsellor for more than a decade. Supplied

Kara said South Asian communities faced unique challenges when it came to family harm.

She identified social conditioning around gender roles, beliefs about divorce and its impact on family honour, and the idea that marriage was for life as some of the barriers.

"Immigration and visas are another major challenge," she said.

Kara said many women faced psychological abuse from partners who threatened them over their visa status, including telling them they would not extend or support their residency applications.

Some women were also threatened with being sent back to their home country, she said.

Sahaayta offers a range of programmes, including its Breaking the Cycle programme, which runs for 12 to 14 weeks, trauma counselling and counselling for children.

The organisation works with agencies and entities such as New Zealand Police, Oranga Tamariki, Gandhi Nivas, Family Success Matters, Family Action and Women's Refuge.

Kara said more needed to be done, particularly around interpretation services.

She said the Southeast Asian community was growing in New Zealand, but the workforce needed to support those communities had not kept pace.

She pointed to the Filipino and Rohingya communities as groups that needed more support.

Ranjna Patel, founder of Gandhi Nivas, a community-led initiative addressing family harm in South Auckland, said the problem remained widespread but was often hidden.

"What I've learned from an observer outside of the service is that it is a nationwide problem," she said.

Patel said she initially started Gandhi Nivas believing family harm was primarily a South Asian or Indian problem.

But she later realised it was a much broader issue. Gandhi Nivas now provides services to Māori, Pasifika and European communities, as well as Indian individuals.

"Family harm is a bigger problem, and aggravating factors are not necessarily just the man," she said.

"It is the whole family dynamic, the pressures that come into the home that causes family harm," she said.

"Our philosophy is our biggest contribution, which has seen such a big success in dealing with family harm."

If you are a victim of family violence or in a relationship that makes you fearful about your own or anyone else's safety, seek help as soon as possible.

World.title: Foreign espionage increasing in Pacific, says NZSIS
World.content:
New Zealand's spy agency says it is increasingly coming across espionage activity in the Pacific - and has identified individuals connected to an unnamed foreign intelligence service.

The NZSIS reports that individually, Pacific states remain vulnerable to attempts at subversion, both in politically, and in the community.

Security expert Al Gillespie told RNZ's Midday Report that China has been singled out as a regional threat like never before.

"In previous reports you've seen it also making that point about Russia, or about Iran. But they're not mentioned this time. But China is," he said

"And it's mentioned not just with regards to domestic interference but also with influence in the pacific. And so they;'re trying to shine a light on what may be going on."

The NZSIS said that regionalism and consensus were the best safeguards, which is why foreign actors seek to sow division.

Meanwhile, the SIS also said diaspora community groups in New Zealand were being unfairly targeted by foreign states and their proxies seeking to limit their democratic rights and freedoms.

Gillespie said China was unfortunately not the only country that undertakes this activity.

He said SIS staff spent a lot of time talking to different communities about how the agency functioned and how it would handle threats so people could feel confident about coming to them with their concerns.

World.title: Chinese electric vehicles reshaping New Zealand's car market
World.content:
Chinese-made electric vehicles are reshaping the country's car market.

The value of reduced-emission vehicle imports, including fully electric vehicles, hybrids and plug-in hybrids, rose 33 percent to $2.9 billion in the 12 months to 30 June, accounting for 48 percent of the total value of all passenger vehicles imports, according to the latest Stats NZ figures.

Japan remained the main source of hybrid vehicles, accounting for 63 percent of imports, while China supplied 73 percent of New Zealand's fully electric vehicles.

The Motor Trade Association said 29 Chinese vehicle brands were now represented in New Zealand, including BYD, Chery, Dongfeng, Geely, GWM, Leapmotor and Zeekr.

This count excludes established global automakers that manufacture some electric vehicles in China, including BMW, Cupra, Honda, Kia, Mazda, Mini and Tesla.

It also excludes Volvo, Lotus and Polestar, which are partly Chinese-owned.

Industry experts and vehicle dealers say the influx has expanded consumer choice while challenging long-established Japanese and European brands with lower starting prices, broader model ranges and increasingly sophisticated technology.

Larry Fallowfield, sector manager for dealers and specialist services at the Motor Trade Association Supplied

Market shift

Larry Fallowfield, sector manager for dealers and specialist services at the Motor Trade Association, said the growing presence of Chinese-made vehicles had marked a significant shift in New Zealand's car market in recent years.

He said Chinese brands had expanded consumer choice, while lower prices had encouraged more buyers to consider electric vehicles.

"By lowering that price point, perhaps buyers who were not looking at battery-electric vehicles are now looking at battery-electric vehicles," he said.

"If we look at July this year compared with the previous 12 trading months, there has been ... [an] increase in the number of battery-electric vehicles sold," he said.

"I would suspect that most of those battery-electric vehicles are coming from Chinese manufacturers."

China overtook Japan as New Zealand's largest source of EV imports in 2021. RNZ / Yiting Lin

Fallowfield said the surge in fuel prices, driven by conflict in the Middle East earlier this year, had boosted EV sales.

However, the broader shift towards electrified vehicles had been building for years.

"Over the last five years, rental companies have been buying more electrified vehicles," he said.

"Many of those hybrids eventually end up our in-service market and are then sold to the general public," he said.

"People often start with a hybrid and then move to the next stage of electrification," he said.

"Whether that is a battery-electric vehicle or a plug-in hybrid, those appear to be the areas experiencing the strongest growth."

Fallowfield said New Zealanders' perceptions of Chinese vehicles were changing.

Competitive starting prices had helped Chinese electric vehicles enter the market quickly, he said, while improving quality had helped them maintain their position.

"Traditionally we bought British cars," he said.

"Then Chinese cars started coming in and they were a little bit of an entry level.

"But over time Chinese manufactured vehicles have come into the country with all the technology [found] in established brands - safety features, advanced driving, big touch screens. They are now at that level of quality."

Fallowfield said the next challenges for electric vehicles in the future would be how many of them can survive in the market.

Hayden Johnston, director and general manager of GVI Group RNZ / Yiting Lin

GVI Group, an Auckland-based importer of used Japanese vehicles, has specialised in electric vehicles since 2014.

Hayden Johnston, the company's director and general manager, said New Zealand's vehicle market had changed significantly over the past 12 years.

More distributors and dealers were now offering new electric vehicles, he said, while prices had fallen enough to make electric vehicles accessible to a much broader group of households.

"We were selling first- and second-generation Nissin Leafs," he said. "That was the staple of what was available to us from Japan and the UK at that time.

"They were expensive, a used Nissan Leaf cost around $40,000 at that time, and we were selling to a very specific type of customers.

"But now we've got uptake from the public, EVs are a lot more common and accepted. Almost every manufacturer has at least one EV option now."

Johnston said customer interest in Chinese electric vehicles was also growing as more Chinese-made vehicles entered New Zealand with competitive pricing and increasingly strong product offerings.

He said he believed it was only a matter of time before Chinese brands became dominant players in New Zealand's EV market.

But as competition intensified, he said, not every brand would survive.

"I don't think there's a place for all of them in the New Zealand market, " he said.

"We could also see some of the legacy manufacturers that we are familiar with drop out of the market. New Zealand is not a huge market."

Chinese car manufacturer BYD is competing alongside more established producers such as Nissan. RNZ / Yiting Lin

Crowded market

According to the Motor Trade Association's latest New Zealand Vehicle Fleet and Industry report, one of the most significant changes in recent years has been the rapid growth in new EV imports from China, including both Chinese brands and vehicles made in China for overseas manufacturers.

Japan was New Zealand's largest source of EV imports in 2020, but China overtook it in 2021.

China accounted for 10 percent of New Zealand's EV imports in 2020.

Its share rose to 58 percent in 2022 before easing to 42 percent in 2024.

The trend reflects China's growing role in the global electric vehicle industry.

The report said China now accounted for 70 percent of global EV production, with Chinese brands making up 80 percent of that output.

China also accounted for 40 percent of global EV exports in 2024, and Chinese brands made up 70 percent of those exports.

The rise in Chinese-made EV imports has brought a growing number of Chinese brands into New Zealand's increasingly crowded market, a trend the report said was likely to continue.

BYD, a Chinese EV manufacturer that entered the New Zealand market in 2022, sold 152 vehicles in a single day in March.

Warren Willmot, general manager of BYD New Zealand Supplied

Warren Willmot, BYD's New Zealand general manager, said the surge was driven by fears that the government might impose restrictions on vehicle use and that fuel supplies could run short because of conflict in the Middle East.

He said orders had since fallen considerably but remained well above the levels recorded before the conflict.

Willmot said BYD had faced supply constraints in recent months because of the global fuel crisis and shipping disruptions.

A small number of customers had waited up to three months for their vehicles, he said, but more than 2700 vehicles were arriving in August, helping to ease the backlog.

Established EV car manufacturers are struggling to compete with cheaper Chinese brands. RNZ / Yiting Lin

Willmot said that although New Zealand's vehicle market had become increasingly crowded, more Chinese manufacturers were still preparing to enter.

He agreed that not every brand would ultimately survive, including some Chinese brands.

"Some Chinese brands think entering export markets will help them survive," he said.

"It's not going to be the case. The same can also be said of some established Western and Japanese brands," he said.

"Nissan, Mitsubishi and Volkswagen are all under pressure," he added.

"Even this month, we have seen KGM, a South Korean brand, and LDV, a Chinese brand, pull out in New Zealand market."

Willmot said BYD's founder and chairman, Wang Chuanfu, expected a period of global reconciliation in the automotive industry, with about 30 percent of the brands currently in the market likely to withdraw from the marker within the next two years.

Chinese automaker Dongfeng Motor entered the New Zealand market in late 2025 with three fully electric models, led by the compact Box hatchback, which was priced from under $30,000.

Simon Rutherford, chief executive of Auto Distribution Holdings, the company that introduced Dongfeng to New Zealand Supplied

Simon Rutherford, chief executive of Auto Distribution Holdings, the company that introduced Dongfeng to New Zealand, said competitive pricing alone would not be enough to succeed.

Brands also needed to offer strong overall value and a compelling ownership experience, he said.

"We are well on our way to our first 1000-unit sales milestone and have already delivered more than 900 vehicles," he said.

Rutherford said there was still room for new brands in New Zealand, but their survival would depend on whether they could achieve sufficient sales volume, build market share and operate sustainably alongside established global competitors.

"There will be consolidation and changes across both retail and distribution channels deployed in the market," he said.

"Some long-established brands will shrink, while others will grow rapidly. But that is a win for consumers, because so many companies are now competing for their business."

BMW electric vehicles at a charging station in Shanghai, China. GAO YUWEN

The Motor Trade Association report noted that, in China, nearly all small electric cars were priced below the average small internal-combustion vehicle, including petrol and diesel models.

Prices fell significantly across most vehicle segments between 2023 and 2024, driven in part by lower battery costs.

The report said battery prices were expected to keep falling over the next few years because of an oversupply of lithium and continued expansion in battery manufacturing capacity.

That could further reduce EV purchase prices in New Zealand, particularly for vehicles imported from China, and accelerate the electrification of the country's vehicle fleet.

Fallowfield said price was a major factor in encouraging consumers to consider electric vehicles, but quality, servicing and after-sales support would also shape their decisions.

He said Chinese manufacturers were likely to remain major players in New Zealand, although whether they would come to dominate the market would depend on which brands survived.

"I think they are established enough now that they will continue to grow," he said.

"Probably not at the same rate as they have over the past couple of years. That growth will start to slow.

World.title: Brian To'o is still just the beginning for the PNG Chiefs
World.content:
After a week in the spotlight following the biggest decision of his career, Brian To'o went back to work.

His showing in the Panthers' 12-6 loss to the Roosters was typical of the To'o we've come to know.

The future Papua New Guinea Chief did not bring up his 100th try for the Panthers but did churn through 17 runs for 162 metres to go with five tackle busts and two line breaks. For some wingers that's a big night but for To'o it's the standard.

'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate Two of the NRL's most successful modern coaches weigh into the debate about the concessions afforded to the league's forthcoming PNG franchise.

The performance came in the days following confirmation of To'o's move to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs and it shouldn't have been a surprise.

There are good reasons To'o has become the premier winger of his time, and having such a high baseline is one of them.

Continued excellence on his part, for both the rest of this season and his final year with Penrith in 2027, is as close to a given as you'll find anywhere in rugby league.

He is the best player the Chiefs have signed but that may not remain so. Not since the Broncos filled their boots with Queensland-based stars for their inaugural season in 1988 has an expansion team signed so much established talent.

Zac Lomax will return to rugby league with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Brendon THorne)

Of the six players to commit to the Chiefs, four have played State of Origin in the past two years. Some clubs go decades without signing one or two players who fit such a criteria.

The other two are the greatest try-scorer the Australian game has ever known and one of England's top front-rowers.

Unless Joseph Manu was just in Port Moresby on holiday, it seems likely they'll add the Golden Boot winner from the most recent World Cup to the list before long.

They have achieved all this without really entering the cut and thrust of the transfer market in earnest. Officially, the Chiefs cannot talk to any NRL free agents for the 2028 season until November 1 this year.

Manu has been linked with an NRL return with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Each of the signings they've made within the NRL have come because a club granted permission for the player in question to negotiate early or because the player activated something in their contract that allowed them to do so.

They've done all this while the luxury compound they're building is still a hole in the ground and before they have a logo or a jersey. To'o himself hasn't even been to Papua New Guinea before.

They're yet to land any young legs but if these are the players they can sign through the activation of obscure clauses and arcane options and the like, imagine what they can do in the jungle of true free agency when they have the biggest and sharpest teeth via their mountain of government funding?

With local products like Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finlay Glare, all of whom are enjoying standout seasons with London Broncos and will eventually take up development contracts with the club, to fill out the other end of the roster, the Cheifs can keep aiming high.

The floodgates have yet to truly open but already the ripples of the league's new money-monster are clear to see.

Hudson Young, fresh off a career-changing State of Origin series, is in the Chiefs' sights and despite the Raiders offering just about everything they've got to a player who has found a home in Canberra, fans there are turning as green as their jerseys because they know there's a chance they'll be money-whipped.

Young is the latest player to come into PNG's sights. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The spectre of similar moves loom over a sport addicted to transfer gossip and sank into Thursday's top-of-the-table clash because after the start they've made, no player seems out of reach for the Chiefs.

Not Sam Walker, who turned down the Roosters first contract offer midweek and has the chance to secure untold riches over the final stages of this season, a chance he has surely enhanced after a mature performance that helped put the Tricolours on top of the ladder.

Not Liam Martin, who rattled Cody Ramsey with the best shot of the night or Spencer Leniu, who struggled to find the fire against his former club and looks like he'd benefit from a change of scenery.

Not even Nathan Cleary, who tried every trick he knew but could not break down a resolute Roosters defensive line.

As impossible as it seems to picture him playing rugby league in anything but a Penrith jersey, even he is in play.

Through their tax-free contracts and the legitimacy that comes with signing established stars, the Chiefs have the capability to tip the entire league on its head.

They can pay a battler like a prince, a prince like a king and a king like a god and given they've already shown a taste for the finer things in assembling their roster, there's little reason to expect it won't continue.

Their advantages warp the salary cap beyond recognition and each signing they make is further proof of concept that the gold rush is real.

General manager of football Michael Chammas says he wears it as a badge of honour that clubs are beginning to gripe at the advantages PNG have been given and well may he, given how those clubs, blinded by the glittering of gold, let a Chief into the henhouse.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

It is hard to begrudge any player for taking what's on offer, like it's hard to begrudge the way Chammas and the Chiefs are going about it. They're playing by the rules they've been given and they're playing by them well.

Ever since Jarome Luai was announced as their first signing, their power has become more and more real and it continues to solidify with every signing they make. Now, they are securing a firm foothold on the high side of an uneven surface.

To'o is the latest, but not the last and rugby league is only just beginning to reckon with the power of what the NRL has created with its concessions to the Chiefs and how it alters the competitive balance of the league.

They have turned the dial as far as it will go and are now waiting to see what happens next, as is their way, and it is happening hard and fast all around us.

The downpour of money is a monsoon that shows no sign of breaking, even as rival clubs get swamped.

And stars like To'o who have been swept along are still just the start. Expect plenty more to dive in.

World.title: Teen Italian star breaks world record for second time this week
World.content:
Italian teenage swimming sensation Sara Curtis has broken the world 50m backstroke world record again, just a day after eclipsing the global mark of Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

The 19-year-old Curtis ‌won gold in 26.56 seconds in the final of the European Championships in Paris on Thursday, local time, clipping another 0.07 seconds off the time of 26.63 she had set in Wednesday's semifinals.

That time had obliterated the three-year-old mark of five-time Olympic champion McKeown, who had clocked 26.86 when winning a World Cup race in Budapest in 2023.

Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown backstroke world record Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

It continued the historic week for the Savigliano-born Curtis, who has a Nigerian mother and Italian father, as she becomes the first Black swimmer to hold an individual long-course world record.

Mary-Ambre Moluh, from ​France, finished ‌half a second behind Curtis ​to take the silver, while Britain's Lauren Cox took ​bronze.

"I'm happy I managed it again. It's absurd, another crazy feat," Curtis told Italian TV station Rai 2.

It ​was the ​third medal in Paris for ‌the University of Virginia star, who also took bronze in 100m freestyle and silver in ​the 4x100m freestyle relay.

The teenager had been inching towards the ​world ​record all year, having ​broken the Italian and ‌European records earlier in the season.

"From the moment I set off for Virginia, that's all I thought about, the record. A dream and ​an immense goal," she admitted.

But it has been a tough spell for McKeown, who had to pull out of both the recent Commonwealth Games and the current Pan Pacific Championships because of glandular fever.

The 25-year-old is determined to get back into top shape for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, where Curtis shapes to be one of the pool stars.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki claimed the European 200m breaststroke gold, continuing his terrific rise.

The 18-year-old was fresh from winning gold for Jersey at the Commonwealth Games, only the second ever for his little Channel Island home.

AAP

World.title: Four-goal Austin gives Dees perfect start to new AFLW era
World.content:
Melbourne's new dawn in the AFLW has begun with a win, with recruit Mia Austin kicking four goals to give Demons coach Tom Wilson victory in his first match in charge.

Hawthorn tested last year's preliminary finalists at Princes Park on Thursday night, and went into the final quarter level.

But the Dees kept the Hawks scoreless in the final term to secure a 19-point round one triumph.

AFLW double-header season opener left fans with 'lots of mixed feelings' The AFLW opened its 2026 season with a double-header at Docklands Stadium.

The contest was the first time Melbourne's women have not been coached by Mick Stinear, who is now in charge at Geelong, with Wilson taking over to start his AFLW coaching career.

Liv Purcell returned from the knee reconstruction that kept her to only two games last season and she was best afield, racking up 32 possessions and nine tackles.

Recruited from Carlton, Austin was outstanding and looks the ideal replacement for Eden Zanker, now at Fremantle.

Melbourne captain Kate Hore also starred, but goal kicking let her down and she finished with a wasteful 1.4.

The Hawks rallied after a slow start as they unveiled their key-forward double act, with former Gold Coast player Jacqueline Dupuy joining All-Australian Aine McDonagh.

Dupuy took nine marks and kicked a goal, while McDonagh made a strong start with three majors.

Hawthorn defender Jenna Richardson, who took 11 marks, and ruck Lucy Wales impressed.

With Hore, Tayla Harris and Purcell firing, the Dees threatened to kill off the game early.

Melbourne kicked the first three goals of the game and were up by 23 late in the opening term.

But Dupuy kicked her first for the Hawks to keep them within 17 points at the first change.

The game flipped in the second, as Dupuy and McDonagh fired in attack. Hawthorn kicked three goals to one and only trailed by seven points at the main break.

Jacinta Hose's long-overdue AFLW debut ended in more pain for the Demons' ruck when she was forced out of the game in the second quarter with an ankle injury.

Hose was drafted in 2023, but two knee reconstructions have stalled her career.

When McDonagh kicked the only goal of the third quarter, the Hawks led for the first time in the game and scores were tied at the final change.

But Austin kicked her fourth goal at the start of the last quarter and Elizabeth McNamara added another a couple of minutes later to steady for Melbourne.

While Shelley Heath goaled 11 minutes into the term, the Demons had a three-goal break and the game was over.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Cherry-Evans confirms NRL exit in shock call after Roosters win
World.content:
Daly Cherry-Evans has given himself every chance to book-end his NRL career with a second premiership after confirming 2026 will be his last season in Australia.

The Sydney Roosters star announced today he would finish in the NRL at season's end, before moving to the English Super League for a one-year swan song at Hull FC.

His exit will bring the curtain down on one of the NRL's most storied careers, after debuting at Manly in 2011 before his shock Sea Eagles exit at the end of last season.

At the age of 37, Cherry-Evans is the second-most-capped player in NRL history and has a string of records, including the most 40-20s ever kicked, most golden-point winners and most field goals in the NRL era.

He also captained both Queensland and Australia, helping lead the Maroons to three series wins and claiming a Clive Churchill Medal in 2013.

Cherry-Evans led the Maroons to three series victories as captain. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

His announcement comes despite him showing last night he is still playing as well as ever, scoring both of the Roosters' tries in a 12-6 win over Penrith.

After beginning his career with a premiership as a rookie halfback at Manly in 2011, Cherry-Evans now has the Roosters in first with a second title looking a real possibility.

"I still have a real desire to play and compete, so the opportunity to join Hull FC and experience the Super League is something I'm genuinely excited about," Cherry-Evans said.

"But there's still plenty of football to be played this season, and that's where my focus is.

"We've got a lot we still want to achieve as a team here at the Roosters, and I'm determined to give my all and play my part in that."

Rumours of Cherry-Evans' Super League move had come as something of a shock earlier this week.

Hull will be coached next season by Steve McNamara, who is a long-time friend and former assistant of Roosters' coach Trent Robinson.

The former Queensland halfback shocked Manly last March when he announced he would leave the club after 15 seasons there.

He insisted today he had no ill feelings towards the Sea Eagles, where he remains the most-capped player in the club's history.

"Manly will always hold a special place for me and my family," he said.

Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months There's a new name at the top of the NRL ladder for the first time since March after the Roosters outlasted Penrith in a possible grand final preview.

"I spent more than 15 years there, made lifelong friendships and was fortunate to experience so much throughout my time at the club.

"Coming to the Roosters this year gave me the opportunity to challenge myself in a completely new environment, and I've loved being part of this club."

Cherry-Evans' Roosters arrival has prompted the Tri-colours to deploy promising playmaker Hugo Savala in the centres this season.

Robinson described coaching Cherry-Evans as a "gift" after his side climbed to first and moved to within touching distance of the minor premiership.

"You talk about external motivation, but to watch someone care about the way that he plays the game and goes about it," Robinson said.

"Maybe two or three years ago at a charity function, I almost bought his boot for a couple of thousand dollars, but one of my mates got it before me.

"I feel like a guy plays with a spirit… I really enjoy watching him play, and I've said that, but I've enjoyed watching him come and want to improve his game."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: King could beat Longmuir to AFL's coach of the year gong
World.content:
Melbourne's stunning win over Fremantle was more than a statement.

It was the destruction of any sentiment that the Demons have been punching above their weight, and a warning that they are a true contender.

For first-year coach Steven King, it was also confirmation that he is the main threat to Justin Longmuir's status as the AFL's coach of the year.

Considering the latter's success so far in 2026, that is quite an achievement.

Christian Petracca left Melbourne at the end of 2025. (Getty images: Morgan Hancock)

When Melbourne sacked premiership coach Simon Goodwin four years after a drought-breaking flag, and then lost Norm Smith medallist Christian Petracca and four-time best and fairest winner Clayton Oliver to rival clubs, nobody thought the Demons would bounce back this emphatically.

Now they are fighting for a top-four finish and have scored more than 100 points in four of their past six games, despite losing star forward Brody Mihocek to a season-ending neck injury.

New structure on old foundation

The belief at Melbourne is palpable.

"If we play our brand of footy we can beat anyone. That's the belief Kingy's driving in us," Harrison Petty told ABC Sport after the Demons' win over Fremantle.

"We play a brutal game of footy and we try to play with a bit of flair. In previous years we haven't done that, and this year it's changed. It's an exciting brand."

After the victory, King credited Goodwin for paving the way to the side's success.

Simon Goodwin was sacked last August. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

"I think you missed the foundations of what was already here," he said.

"They won a premiership five years ago.

" Simon Goodwin was a great coach of this footy club. So I've walked into a group that knows how to compete around the footy and defend. "

His sentiments are reflected in the Demons' statistics.

Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly A raft of AFL rule changes for the 2026 season have either excited or horrified a range of fans — Cody Atkinson and Sean Lawson examine the changes and whether they have had the desired impact.

Melbourne already boasted a competitive midfield that was fourth for clearance differential and first for contested possession differential last season, but it fell down in its ball movement.

In 2026, Steven King has overcome the loss of the club's two best midfielders and still improved to third for transition, first for clearance differential and sixth for inside-50 differential.

Their only weakness is in defence, sitting 14th for points against.

Does King beat Longmuir?

So what makes a coach of the year? Is it surmounting numerous obstacles to rise up the ladder? Or should it be the leader of the best side of the season?

Longmuir has put the Dockers in the box seat for their second-ever minor premiership, lifting the side from sixth to first in his seventh season.

Justin Longmuir makes a strong case to be the AFL's coach of the year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The football gods have smiled on him with a league-high 11 players featuring in every game this season and the likelihood of at least five players in the All-Australian squad.

But how can you argue against the figurehead of a side that has had three losses, a club-record 14-game win streak and is two games clear at the top of the table, being crowned the game's best coach?

Of the 23 winners of coach of the year, 39 per cent have won the premiership, 56 per cent have made the grand final and 78 per cent have made the top four — supporting the argument ladder position is a key factor.

How the Hawks are making their two-ruck strategy work Once thought to be dead and buried, the era of the dual ruck has been resuscitated by a handful of clubs in finals contention, including Hawthorn.

More than 80 per cent of winners rose up the ladder, but the four first-year winners did not make a grand final that same season.

Winning the accolade is a massive sign of future success, with 11 of the 16 winners delivering a flag after receiving the gong.

It is a debate that will divide the footy community across the next fortnight, but neither coach will be anxious about the winner.

Longmuir's Dockers are the premiership favourite but are now batting away doubters following their loss at the MCG.

King's Dees, meanwhile, feel like the dark horse who could not only shape September but might just finish the month with the grandest prize of all.

World.title: Britain's Super League says NRL has made formal investment offer
World.content:
Britain's Super League has revealed it has received an investment offer from the NRL as Australian involvement in British rugby league's premier tournament appeared to take a significant step closer.

Talks have been going on for months between representatives of the Australian and British games, but today's announcement represented the first time Super League had received a formal offer.

"RL Commercial can confirm that a first offer has been received from the ARLC (the Australian Rugby League Commission, which governs the NRL in Australia) as part of the sport's recapitalisation project," Rugby League Commercial said in a statement.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

"The Super League clubs have been informed this morning.

"Details of the offer remain confidential."

Super League has made no bones about its urgent need for financial support and investment, while the NRL has been equally insistent on its vision to help make the European game stronger in a push to make rugby league much stronger globally.

Some reports have suggested that Super League could receive a huge investment of about $60 million over the next five years from the NRL, with the Australian league eventually owning 50 per cent of its UK counterpart.

The NRL's former chief executive Andrew Abdo, who's now taken up the same role at Tennis Australia, had been instrumental in the move towards the "globalisation" of rugby league and on a visit to Britain in April, spoke about the NRL's hoped-for involvement in Super League.

"We really believe in the globalisation of rugby league," Abdo said.

"This is a great game, and we want to take it to as many people as possible. We want to win as many fans as possible.

"So while the game is growing really well in the southern hemisphere, we also want the game to be strong here in the north.

"This is about a partnership where we can collaborate on how we can grow the game, how we can grow revenues, and how those revenues can be pumped back into the game.

"That's pretty nuanced, and that's something we have to develop together."

The Super League is moving into its business end this season with the play-offs set for next month and the grand final to be held on October 3 at Old Trafford.

AAP

World.title: Australian teen golfer Jessica Bang dies in Thailand
World.content:
Teenage Australian golfer Jessica Bang has died in Thailand after suffering a brain haemorrhage.

The 18-year-old collapsed on August 1, as reported by the Daily Telegraph, before being rushed to Synphaet Ramintra Hospital in Bangkok.

WPGA Tour of Australasia announced Bang's death in a statement on Thursday night.

"The WPGA Tour of Australasia and the broader Australian golf community is deeply saddened by the passing of young Tour member Jessica Bang in Thailand," the statement read.

"The thoughts and prayers of everyone at the WPGA Tour of Australasia and the broader Australian golf community are with Jessica's family, friends and all those who knew and loved her at this incredibly difficult time."

Bang was in Thailand preparing to play in the International Qualifying Tournament for the Korean women's professional tour.

In just her fifth professional start, Bang won her first tournament in February, the Women's NSW Open Regional Qualifying Event at Moss Vale.

Bang won by five shots, including an eight-under final round 65, which set a new course record at Moss Vale Golf Club, as reported by Australian Golf Digest.

World.title: Long careers increase risk of brain damage, but is informed consent enough?
World.content:
The secret document that Geelong defender Jake Kolodjashnij signed to release his club from any legal risk over future concussions has opened an enormous can of worms.

That is aside from the ethical considerations, the conflict of interest faced by the AFL chairman, Craig Drummond, who was Geelong president at the time, and the Cats' response to why they did not lodge the document with the AFL.

What the incident does shine a light on is the logical extension of sanctioning high-collision sports.

Because the truth is, by allowing people to play contact sport, particularly at the elite level, they are exposed to a life of potential brain injuries and chronic pain.

Neurophysiologist and concussion researcher Alan Pearce from Swinburne University found the longer professional athletes participated in certain contact sports, at any level, the greater their chance of some form of brain trauma.

His findings sparked a realisation involving multiple swear words.

"I say 'holy f***" a lot," he told ABC Sport.

"As I progressed with the increasing of the numbers, I began to realise that there is a spectrum of damage that players were getting.

"This is something that's going to happen to everyone who plays this sport for a long period of time."

Professor Alan Pearce is a leading researcher on concussion in sport. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

For some it was micro damage that would not affect a person's quality of life, but for others it was more serious.

"So, how do we accept a certain amount of damage that is not going to significantly affect the rest of their life or even cut their life short?" Professor Pearce asked.

He and his colleagues published the work earlier this year in the Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology, studying 113 retired male professional Australian rules, rugby league and rugby union players, aged between 28 and 68.

They found that it was the length of a player's total career, not the length of their professional career, nor the number of concussions they suffered, that was the problem.

Consider someone starting Aussie rules as a 10-year-old, getting drafted when they are 18, but then continuing to play long after they retire from the professional game.

Professor Pearce had some test subjects who had played at various levels for 35 years.

The damage was not necessarily caused by major concussions; it was the constant sub-concussive knocks that were the problem.

What does this mean for professional contact sports?

When someone signs a professional contract to play Aussie Rules, or another collision sport, they are potentially signing up to future brain damage.

That is not to mention any number of other risks: An ACL injury, the likelihood of a knee or hip replacement at an early age, the possibility of chronic pain or injuries that restrict a person's lifestyle and career.

There is a risk of sustaining many different types of serious injuries when playing professionally. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

This is the price they pay, but is it worth the cost?

"It's like this unspoken acceptance of professional sport," Professor Pearce said.

"It goes beyond healthy living; in some ways professional sport is extreme sport."

Which raises a difficult question the AFL and other codes are facing: How do you run a sport where there is an implicit risk of brain damage for participants?

Acknowledgement of risk

Which brings us back to the document that Kolodjashnij signed and that Geelong did not think necessary to run by the AFL.

It has now been reported the document was titled "Voluntary Assumption of Risk" and stated: "You take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury of any kind arising directly or indirectly as a result of concussion sustained by you following your decision."

There may be a myriad of problems with what happened, but the concept of an acknowledgement of risk is not so far-fetched.

Kolodjashnij signed the concussion waiver with the Cats in 2024. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Anyone undertaking surgery signs a consent form. It does not absolve a surgeon of gross negligence or malpractice — you cannot break the law or contract your way out of legislation.

But consent effectively protects surgeons from foreseeable events that may occur in surgery, like an infection.

The idea is that people go into the surgery fully aware of the potential risks.

Have we reached a point, given what we know about the dangers of concussion in collision sports, that players may need to sign a consent form when they take up a professional sports contract?

Professor Pearce thinks so; not to absolve clubs and the AFL of responsibility, but for ethical reasons.

"So that everyone knows everything up front," he said.

"It's also about risks of ACL and other injuries. I don't know if young players understand the psychological stress that they're going to be under."

The AFL's concussion protocol says players must be sidelined for at least 12 days before returning. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

At present, there is nothing in the AFL standard players' contract or the players' collective bargaining agreement that spells out the potential risks of the game.

There is a view in the industry that the AFL's education on concussion adequately covers the danger of head knocks so that explicit consent isn't necessary.

Professor Pearce said the expectation is that the AFL should do all it can to minimise the chances of players getting concussed and for clubs to play their part.

He cited monitoring loads through the use of smart mouthguards, placing limits on kids playing football and limiting contact training.

The latter was a recommendation of the Victorian State Coroner, John Cain, from his findings into the death of the former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

The AFL responded in 2024, saying it was implementing that recommendation, although it is still yet to come into place after a long period of collecting training data.

It is understood the AFL is considering limiting contact training from next year.

The bigger picture

Consent would not stop players from suing the AFL or clubs if they have acted negligently.

That is an allegation that will play out in the Supreme Court of Victoria next year, when a class action led by the former Geelong player Max Rooke will hear arguments that he was left with brain damage because of the actions of the AFL and his club.

Rooke has been joined by around 120 former players who are suing the AFL and 11 clubs.

Loading...

This is the bigger picture of the risk facing the entire AFL, and all other collision sports for that matter.

In a writ lodged with the court, Rooke claimed he suffered between 20 and 30 concussions while playing for Geelong, resulting in "life-altering injuries".

This week Margalit Lawyers, acting for the players, signed up two more former players to the class action.

The writ argues the AFL and the clubs failed in their duty of care to enforce rules and protocols around concussion to ensure the players' safety and to avoid exposing them to risk.

"We say that the precautions that we allege should be taken in our statement of claim should have been in place a lot earlier based on medical evidence," special counsel with Margalit Lawyers, Daniel Schram, said.

While Schram believes the AFL should continue to educate players and keep them up to speed with the newest evidence around concussion, he doesn't believe a consent form is the way to go.

Neither does the University of Melbourne Law Professor, Jack Anderson.

"We do know that there is a risk there and the players do agree to that to a certain extent," he said.

"It's an implied consent."

But he said the risk shouldn't be placed on the players.

"The risk should lie with the AFL to make the game as safe as it possibly can."

Tech.title: Apple and Epic argue over how much Apple should get from purchases made outside the App Store
Tech.content:
Apple’s filing is in, and Apple admitted that under the Ninth Circuit’s definition of “necessary costs” they would charge 0% for purchases made via linkouts to the web.

Apple proposed linkout fees of 15% for standard apps and 5% for Small Business Program apps. Epic believes these fees are far outside of the bounds of the Ninth Circuit’s guidance on permissible fees, and we have roughly 60 days to file our opposition supported by expert witnesses.

Tech.title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android.

It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complecte access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years.

But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them.

First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed.

These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. Images: Google

“That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen.

Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted.

“Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so.

Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page.

That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Evan. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal appstore search results.

Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked.

Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water.

“We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and ten things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for.

“Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said.

The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

Tech.title: The fight over Flock and other ALPRs
Tech.content:
There are over 120,000 of Flock’s automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras installed all over the US. Flock’s cameras, and others like them, use AI to identify and track vehicles based on their license plate number, make, model, color, and other info, networked together to track vehicles and people’s movements throughout the day and across the country.

Dozens of communities have canceled contracts for the cameras or turned them off, including Los Angeles, as officials have pushed for more limits on the data they collect, who has access to it, and how it can be used in the future. Earlier this year, Amazon-owned Ring canceled a partnership with Flock after online backlash.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s Clippy-like Mico character is no longer the face of Copilot
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft Copilot will no longer show its emotive yellow blob, Mico, when you use the chatbot’s voice mode. In a support page, Microsoft says it’s going to move Mico to its Learn Live platform, where the avatar will have “more to react to,” as reported earlier by GeekWire.

Mico launched in Copilot’s voice mode last October, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman pitching the avatar as a way to give the chatbot an “identity.” The blob would react to what you say in real-time, complete with facial expressions and animations.

Mico joins the long list of virtual helpers that Microsoft has retired over the years, like Clippy, Cortana, and Rover. “Mico helped us learn about warmth, expressiveness, and how people want to talk with AI,” Microsoft’s support page says. “Those learnings are shaping Copilot going forward.” Microsoft is removing Mico from Copilot “in waves.”

The change is part of Microsoft’s plans to merge its Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot apps. It also comes just months after an AI reshuffling that put Jacob Andreou in charge of Copilot, while Suleyman turned his attention to developing new AI models.

Tech.title: Netflix is closing two game studios
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix plans to shut down two of its gaming studios, as reported by Game File and Variety, as it makes a bigger shift toward party games and titles streamed to TVs.

One of the studios being shut down is Night School Studio, creators of the Oxenfree series. Netflix bought Night School in 2021, and it just released a horror experience called Unhinged for TVs and launched a mobile game in 2025 tied to Black Mirror. The other studio that’s set to close is Helsinki-based Moonloot Games, which was created in 2022.

Netflix’s big push into TV-based games kicked off late last year and was a pivot from a mobile-focused approach that featured prestige indie titles. But Netflix has let many of those indie hits leave its mobile lineup as it focuses instead on four pillars of kids, party, narrative, and “mainstream” games.

“As we continue to prioritize these areas, we see an opportunity to be more focused in our execution, so we are making organizational changes to the business to match those priorities,” Netflix spokesperson Chrissy Kelleher tells The Verge. Netflix is also eliminating “some” additional roles in its games business, according to Kelleher. The cuts include Tara Voelker, who says she was the “single accessibility person” on the gaming team.
